findings.title: Constellation too dim on light mode (lines ≈0.12 effective, ghost); dark mode fine at 0.92
findings.evidence: V06 audit; constellation.ts draw(); deck.css --constellation-alpha 0.72→0.92 light / 0.92→1.0 dark; math: 0.17*0.72=0.12 ghost
findings.rootCause: Global --constellation-alpha multiplier (0.72 light / 0.92 dark) applied uniformly to all draw calls; lattice lines have lowest base alpha (0.17*t≈0.17); at 0.72 they read at 0.12 on cream ground, below perception threshold. Nodes (alpha 1.0) and anomaly ring (drawn at globalAlpha=1) are OK, but structural lines vanish.
findings.proposal: F.W4: Option A (simplest): raise global alpha to 0.92 light / 1.0 dark. Lines reach 0.17*0.92=0.156 light, 0.17*1.0=0.17 dark — visible without competing with type. Anomaly tether 0.28*0.92=0.26 clearly readable. Option B (nuanced, glass-ui coordination): add --constellation-line-boost (default 1.5) that multiplies ONLY line strokes in constellation.ts: ctx.globalAlpha = (red ? 0.26*t+0.07 : 0.17*t) * this.alpha * this.lineBoost. Then --constellation-line-boost: 1.6 light / 1.3 dark. Both preserve node/ring dims while brightening lines. Do NOT layout-shift constellation away from type to compensate — the two goals are orthogonal; E anchor-relative drift is correct.

findings.area: AU tranche dock-animation soundness audit
findings.summary: AU.W2's opacity-lockstep fold (already shipped at commit 89b97ca) unified the timing of container resize and child fade from disparate curves (--dock-motion-fast 0.2s vs --dock-motion-resize 0.3s snappy spring) to a single source token. However, the user reports the dock still exhibits non-iOS-smooth motion with items appearing to lag—container shrinks before children fade—suggesting the fix addressed TIMING parity (both now on --dock-motion-resize) but not ANIMATION QUALITY (spring curve fidelity, easing overshoot, or perceptual lockstep). W8's reka-Tabs+a11y+rail-indicator scope is architecturally correct but orthogonal to the animation quality gap. The audit finds: (1) AU.W2's gate `proof:dock-opacity-lockstep` is a static same-source-token proof, not a perception-level timing probe—it passes because both animate on the same token, not because they FEEL synchronized; (2) the --spring-snappy curve may be insufficient for iOS-grade motion (minimal overshoot, long settle tail); (3) the children reflow during width animation independent of opacity curve shape, creating a visual desync even with matched timing; (4) AU.W8 should NOT be re-scoped to fix animation quality—W8 is specifically a11y/ARIA/vocabulary/indicator work, per the dock-design spec. Instead, a NEW W8.5 or W9-adjacent dock-ANIMATION overhaul (re-evaluated spring curve, opacity+scale timing, or containment-based layout isolation) should be POST-W8 and BEFORE W9, unblocking the slides-supply items. W9/W10 items are all publish-blocking or deferrable as currently categorized; no re-scoping needed there.

findings.title: AU.W2 opacity-lockstep gate is timing-static, not perception-verified
findings.evidence: commit 89b97ca dock.css:424-449 (both .dock-layer{,-item-host} and .dock-layer.layer-active now ride --dock-motion-resize); PROGRESS.md line 52 cites `proof:dock-opacity-lockstep` green as 'same-source-token' proof; the gate script scripts/proof-dock-opacity-lockstep.mjs is a string-match verification (--dock-motion-fast→--dock-motion-resize replacement), NOT a visual settlement probe
findings.rootCause: The proof gate validates that both opacity and container-width animate on the same CSS variable token, ensuring no timing skew at the TOKEN level. However, 'both on --dock-motion-resize' ≠ 'visually synchronized'—the spring curve shape (--spring-snappy has ~1% overshoot + long settle tail, line 159 tokens.css) and the LAYOUT reflow of children during width animation create a perceptual desync even with matched duration/timing-function. iOS springs typically exhibit 15–30% overshoot with faster settle (ζ ≈ 0.3–0.5); --spring-snappy is minimal-overshoot (ζ ≈ 0.8+).
findings.proposal: Replace the static same-source-token gate with a PLAYWRIGHT timing probe: mount the dock, trigger collapse, and measure (via getComputedStyle + requestAnimationFrame sampled positions) the VISUAL settlement frame-by-frame. The probe logs the frame when container width stops changing AND the frame when children opacity reaches 0.01 (near-invisible threshold). A pass asserts both settle within ±1 frame. The NEW gate `proof:dock-motion-visual-parity` joins the existing token gate; they are distinct concerns (syntactic vs perceptual). This unblocks W8 and reveals whether the animation quality issue is curve-shape or layout-isolation.

findings.title: Spring curve (--spring-snappy) may be under-damped for dock motion feel
findings.evidence: tokens.css:159 --spring-snappy is a minimal-overshoot linear() (reaches 1.0 at ~48%, then holds 1.0 plateau to 100%); iOS UX springs (e.g., Apple's system springy, UIView.animate spring) typically overshoot 15–30% with faster settlement. The user report 'NOT springy/iOS' suggests the curve feels mechanical/linear rather than lively.
findings.rootCause: --spring-snappy was tuned for the FLIP morph (low overshoot to avoid jank on rapid re-triggers); the dock reuses it for UI spring feel, where higher overshoot + faster settle reads as more responsive. The curve is CORRECT for FLIP concurrency but SUB-OPTIMAL for UX spring feedback. The two needs diverge: FLIP safety (low overshoot to avoid intermediate-state artifact on re-trigger) vs dock UX (high overshoot for liveliness).
findings.proposal: Author a NEW token --spring-dock (distinct from --spring-snappy) tuned to ~20% overshoot and ζ ≈ 0.5 settle time, mirroring iOS system springs. Update --dock-resize-spring to route through it. The curve is derived from the same linear() generator (value.js spring solver) to ensure pixel-perfect consistency. Gate it with `proof:dock-spring-curve` (plot the curve, verify overshoot ∈ [15%, 30%] + settle time ≤ 0.35s). This is a TUNING change (same motion duration, different curve shape) and is ISOMORPHIC to the existing animation (no breaking changes to ARIA, semantics, or layout).

findings.title: Children reflow during width morph creates layout-cascade desync with opacity
findings.evidence: dock.css:382–385 (.dock-layers has `transition: width ...`); .dock-layer children (flex items) reflow IMMEDIATELY on width change due to flex layout (no containment); the opacity fade happens on a separate property transition, so a slow curve allows visual lag as flex children contract before content opacity reaches 0
findings.rootCause: CSS flex layout reflows children synchronously when width animates (the width change triggers layout recalc). The opacity fade is independent, so even if both are on --dock-motion-resize, the VISUAL EFFECT is: (1) width shrinks, (2) children reflow to fit narrower space, (3) opacity fades in parallel BUT appears to lag because the reflow was instant. iOS springs feel snappy partly because the content SCALES/FADES in lockstep with the container—here, the content reflows (a layout cascade) rather than scaling.
findings.proposal: Two options: (A) **Layout isolation via containment** (AU.W8.5): add `content-visibility: auto` or `contain: layout style paint` to `.dock-layer` (the active/leaving panes). This allows the browser to paint/layout children independently of the container width morph, creating a visual 'box' that fades independently. Requires testing for overflow + scroll stability. (B) **Scale + opacity over width** (AU.W8.5 or W9): instead of animating width (which reflows), animate `scale` on a wrapper + clip the container, fading opacity in tandem. This is a STRUCTURAL change to the FLIP (would need `useLayerTransition` to animate `scale` instead of width for the collapse/expand morph). Option A is lower-risk and isomorphic; option B is higher-fidelity but requires arch rework. Recommend A for W8.5 audit, B deferred to BOOK unless slides demands it.

findings.title: AU.W8 scope (reka-Tabs rail + a11y contract + vocabulary) is correct and orthogonal
findings.evidence: AU.md §4.2 #11–12; AU.W1b-dock.md §1 items 1–5 + §4; the rail-indicator is a VISUAL travelling element (per-button bg retired, replaced by one animated indicator), not an animation-quality fix. The a11y/ARIA contract is STRUCTURAL (role=tablist/tab, aria-selected, roving tabindex), not motion-related. The vocabulary is a NAMING/DOCS convention.
findings.rootCause: The dock-animation quality issue (spring curve + layout reflow) is INDEPENDENT of the structural rail ARIA redesign. W8 correctly targets the STRUCTURE/ACCESSIBILITY/LABELLING layer; animation tuning is a separate concern. Mis-scoping W8 to include animation would couple two independent design domains (accessibility vs motion physics) and delay W8's a11y gate completion.
findings.proposal: DO NOT re-scope AU.W8. Keep it focused on: (1) reka-ui Tabs rail adoption (APG ARIA canon), (2) travelling rail-indicator (CSS animation of one element replacing per-button backgrounds), (3) a11y/state contract test (behavioural vitest for tablist/aria-selected/roving-tabindex, per inv-ε), (4) spring-fidelity unification (the existing --scale-press-dock 0.92→0.96 token change already SHIPPED at 8e4cb9f; no new work), (5) vocabulary + base renames (docs + useDockTouchGate rename + DockTabButton retire). Defer animation-quality tuning to a POST-W8 wave or fold into W9 if slides explicitly blocks on it.

findings.evidence: AU.md §4.3–§4.5: W9 items #17/#20 (size vocab), #21/#22 (dark-ergo), #30/#31 (control-pane), #32 (Drawer :native); all named ≥2 consumers or are paired (size vocab is ONE pass). findings.rootCause: The dock animation quality issue does NOT block any W9 items—none of W9's consumers (speedtest, muster, fourier, slides) list dock-motion-smoothness as a dependency. The issue is a UX refinement, not a blocker. W10's publish is gated only on AU's own green CI (inv-27), not on animation perception.

If the dock-animation issue becomes a PUBLISH blocker (e.g., slides explicitly requests it), fold a spring-curve + layout-containment audit into W9's opening and defer the demo/property slides-supply items to a W9b. Currently, no evidence suggests that. This gates nothing and keeps the plan honest.

risks: The `proof:dock-opacity-lockstep` gate passing does not guarantee perceptual visual sync—a static token-match gate is insufficient for UX-grade motion correctness. Re-opening and running a Playwright timing probe post-W8 is essential to validate before publishing.
Tuning --spring-snappy globally may affect FLIP concurrency safety in other docks or components; --spring-dock should be isolated to --dock-resize-spring only, verified by grep (0 other routes).

Containment rules (contain: layout style paint) are a rendering hint; older browsers (Safari <17) may not respect them, causing reflow to leak. Fallback to option B (scale-based animation) may be necessary if containment proves fragile in testing.

AU.W8's a11y contract test (the re-lettered original W6-dock-b) has a NEW dependency: a mounted-dock behavioural vitest requires real Vue + DOM bindings. Ensure the test scaffold is in place before W8 execution begins; scripted snapshot testing (reka-ui ARIA binding checks) may be insufficient.

findings.area: Gate Fleet Audit: glass-ui + slides Integrity & AU.W8–W10 Gaps
findings.summary: The glass-ui gate manifest (GU/scripts/gates.mjs) is the single source of truth and maintains strict invariant parity with CI at HEAD (32 gates). The manifest itself is well-formed with comprehensive proof:* gates covering AU.W0–W7 work (color leaf, WebGL substrate, blob trio, dock opacity-lockstep, strict-templates keystone, Fraunces ship). However, three critical NEW gates required for AU.W8–W10 are ABSENT from the manifest: proof:dock-a11y-contract (AU.W8, the reka-Tabs rail + tablist/tab/aria-selected a11y binding), proof:dock-vocabulary (AU.W8, the dock README role-name/composable-name registry — the script exists but NOT in gates.mjs), and proof:au-w9-consumers (AU.W9, the ≥2-consumer overfitting bar for lean folds + slides-supply). The AU PROGRESS document enumerates all 21 AU gates with greening waves; only 19 are registered in the manifest. Slides CI is minimal (typecheck + build only; no gate-matrix equivalent exists). No manifest drift at HEAD.

findings.evidence: GU/scripts/proof-dock-vocabulary.mjs exists (lines 1–86, AU.W8 gate script authored, bite-check: delete role from README → red). Gate NOT listed in GU/scripts/gates.mjs (no entry with id='proof:dock-vocabulary'). AU.W1c design registry (GU/docs/tranches/AU/design/AU.W1c-color-gates.md:220) enumerates it as REQUIRED for W8. AU PROGRESS.md (line 58) tags it PLANNED for W8.
findings.rootCause: The proof:dock-vocabulary script was authored as AU.W8 deliverable (re-grounded from the original Charter's ASK-7 clauses on useTouchGate/DockTabButton retirement), but the gates.mjs entry was not added during AU.W1 design-slice registration. The AU.W1c registry (the gate-fleet source of truth) was authored before the W8 script, creating a forward-reference gap.
findings.proposal: Add entry to GATES array in GU/scripts/gates.mjs: `{ id: "proof:dock-vocabulary", cmd: "proof:dock-vocabulary", tags: ["local", "ci"], note: "AU.W8 — the dock README role-name + composable-name vocabulary convention (re-grounded: useTouchGate stays general, DockTabButton kept; the README enumerates 4 roles + useDock* names)" }`. Verify the entry is ci-tagged (so ci.yml step is auto-verified by --verify-ci). Run `npm run gates:verify-ci` to ensure manifest==ci invariant holds.

findings.title: proof:webgl-golden gate DEFERRED in AU.W7 — born-green assumption may not hold
findings.evidence: AU PROGRESS.md line 57 notes: 'proof:webgl-golden DEFERRED (this env's headless Chrome runs only the deterministic capture path — the live-rAF path fails identically for aurora; a reliable blob pixel golden can't run green in CI here. The 8-assertion CPU-equivalence proves the color to float-epsilon + the aurora capture-render verifies the shared substrate's GPU path — together the GPU correctness; the blob zero-perturb pixel golden BOOKs on a stable headless WebGL-live capture).' The gate is enumerated in AU.W1c registry (line 213) as W6,W7 but with a DEFERRED note. NOT in GU/scripts/gates.mjs (no entry).
findings.rootCause: The headless Chrome environment used for CI cannot reliably run live WebGL rasterization; the deterministic capture path (the pre-rendered-frame playback) passes identically before/after the substrate refactor, but a true pixel-golden requires a stable WebGL rasterizer. The gate was designed in AT but deferred in AU pending either (a) a stable headless WebGL2 rasterizer discovery, (b) a platform-specific golden (e.g., SwiftShader determinism lock), or (c) a lower-fidelity golden (e.g., shader-output histogram matching). The CPU-equivalence gate + aurora capture-render together subsume the correctness proof for now.
findings.proposal: BOOK (carry forward) the proof:webgl-golden gate with an explicit DEFERRED note in the AU.W10 close. Do NOT add it to gates.mjs yet. Instead, author a GU/docs/tranches/AU/proof-webgl-golden-DEFERRED.md with: (1) the reason (headless WebGL rasterizer instability), (2) the acceptability condition (CPU-equivalence + capture-render parity = GPU correctness), (3) the trigger for future re-opening (stable rasterizer availability or a platform-specific determinism lock). Reference this DEFERRED note in AU.FINAL.md under 'Known Deferrals'. If a stable rasterizer emerges, author the gate + add to manifest at that time.

findings.title: manifest==ci invariant HOLDS at HEAD (gates:verify-ci green); release set is 17 gates (17/32 subset)
findings.evidence: GU/scripts/gates.mjs lines 95–111 define verifyCi() which parses ci.yml run: npm run X steps and cross-checks against gatesFor('ci'). Command: `npm run gates:verify-ci` outputs '[gates:verify-ci] ci.yml matches the manifest ci set (32 gates).'. Local set: `npm run proof:all` (which runs `node scripts/gates.mjs --run local`) filters to 38+ gates (local-tagged include sibling-local gates). Release set: `node scripts/gates.mjs --list release` outputs 17 gates (release-tagged subset).
findings.rootCause: The as.W2 inv-θ structure ensures structural parity by design: the manifest is the SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH; ci.yml is a thin filtered view (per-step visibility retained for Actions UI); release.sh will be a thin filtered aggregate. No structural drift possible because drift reddens the gates:verify-ci check (which runs in ci.yml as the LAST step before build artifacts are published).
findings.proposal: INVARIANT CONFIRMED. No action needed. Document in AU.FINAL.md: 'The manifest==ci invariant holds at AU.W10 close: gates:verify-ci green; 32 gates ci-tagged; 17 gates release-tagged; full local set (including sibling-local + local-only gates) green.' This is a green checkmark for audit.

risks: The three missing AU.W8–W10 gates (proof:dock-a11y-contract, proof:dock-vocabulary, proof:au-w9-consumers) are not in the manifest yet but ARE enumerated in the AU.W1c registry. If gates.mjs is not updated before W8 lands, the CI will not catch the a11y contract regression + the proof:au-w1-design gate will report a mismatch (the registry enumerates 21 gates but only 18 are manifest-registered).

The proof:webgl-golden gate is DEFERRED with a documented acceptance rationale (CPU-equivalence + capture-render parity). If future audits question why a pixel-golden is absent, the DEFERRED.md document must be maintained and visible; otherwise the deferral will be silently forgotten and re-litigated.

The proof:dock-vocabulary script exists (GU/scripts/proof-dock-vocabulary.mjs) but is NOT wired into gates.mjs. If someone runs `npm run proof:dock-vocabulary` locally, it passes or fails independently of the gating structure, creating a false sense of coverage. Adding it to the manifest makes the coverage explicit and CI-enforced.

AU.W8's atomicity (reka-Tabs rail + travelling-indicator land together) is documented in AU notes but not captured in the manifest structure. findings.area: Keyframes.js Animation Engine Audit for Dock Overhaul
findings.summary: Keyframes.js offers a sophisticated, production-grade animation engine with iOS-style spring physics as its cornerstone, positioned to elevate the glass-ui dock beyond CSS-only transitions. The engine provides: (1) SpringProgress — an analytic second-order damped harmonic oscillator with iOS-canonical (response, dampingFraction) parametrization, supporting three damping regimes (underdamped/critically-damped/overdamped); (2) CSS linear() emission via springLinearStops() for WAAPI delegation with true overshoot/settle on the compositor; (3) AnimationGroup compositor for synchronized multi-property choreography with layer blending; (4) Timeline family for scroll-driven and manual progress tracking; and (5) ElementMorph FLIP helper. The dock's shrink-before-fade desync stems from CSS transition timing divergence (fixed 3× compression, native View-Transition swaps the curve) — the fix is live SpringProgress tracking with unified spring authority. The engine achieves zero-alloc group steady-state (D.W4) and is architected as light (value.js-free springs, morph, timelines) and heavy (CSS parser, WAAPI, live engine). Import surface: await loadAnimationEngine() for the CSS-bearing classes; SpringProgress/springLinearStops/springTimingFunction stay static.

findings.title: SpringProgress: iOS-canonical analytic spring solver available
findings.evidence: keyframes.js/src/animation/spring.ts:1-131 (SpringProgress class declaration); springTimingFunction.ts:40-75 (JS easing generation); springLinearStops.ts:33-73 (CSS linear() emission)
findings.rootCause: The dock today uses fixed-duration CSS transitions (glass-ui/src/styles/dock.css) and hand-tuned cubic-bezier overshoots (--ease-apple-spring), disconnected from the physics engine already available one package import away.
findings.proposal: Import SpringProgress directly for live-target dock width animations. Parametrize with iOS presets: underdamped (response 0.5, ζ 0.85) for expand↔collapse, critically-damped (ζ=1) for show/hide, and snappy (response 0.3, ζ 0.7) for icon press-back. The solver tracks mid-flight target changes (gesture interrupts, tap-while-animating), producing the iOS-grade continuity CSS transitions cannot.
findings.gate: proof:spring-driven — the dock collapse/expand on the live-SpringProgress path settles within 2× the original CSS duration, no visible jitter on interrupt

findings.title: springLinearStops() emits CSS linear() for WAAPI delegation
findings.evidence: keyframes.js/src/animation/springLinearStops.ts:46-73 returns e.g. 'linear(0, 0.234 4.17%, ..., 1)' with intermediate positions capturing spring overshoot/settle; springTimingFunction.ts:105-120 pairs JS .fn easing with .css twin for compositor fallback
findings.rootCause: Glass-ui's native View-Transition path today swaps the spring for a different cubic-bezier (the 'hand-tuned' fork in the C audit). A unified curve requires one authority.
findings.proposal: When AnimationGroup or a manual spring drives dock size, emit the linear() stops once and pass to WAAPI via the .css property. Glass-ui's View-Transition snaps the container + panes via view-transition-name (dock.css), but the size animate itself routes through CSS transition-timing-function — thread the spring's CSS twin there. The two curves (JS driving the iOS-grade gesture, CSS running the compositor) then read from one spring preset, eliminating the fork.
findings.gate: proof:unified-curve — a View-Transition dock expand on both rAF path and native path visually converges to the same settle time (±50ms) with identical overshoot envelope

findings.title: ElementMorph provides FLIP-like position/scale interpolation without hand-rolled setup
findings.evidence: keyframes.js/src/animation/morph.ts:48-100 (ElementMorph class: measure → compute dx/dy/sx/sy at(progress) / toCSSTransform / apply / play); numeric.ts:65-120 (zero-alloc NumericAnimation base)
findings.rootCause: Glass-ui dock layer swap today runs a FLIP sequence manually (useLayerTransition.ts:135-186 fallback path: capture→pin→swap→measure→repin→animate). This is load-bearing but hand-rolled, losing the abstraction benefit.
findings.proposal: Consider ElementMorph as a reusable FLIP abstraction layer for complex dock transitions (layer pane swaps, icon morph into full-screen). Measure from/to elements, call .play(duration), and let NumericAnimation handle the interpolation. This simplifies the manual FLIP logic and unlocks composition patterns (e.g. staggered icon animates while pane cross-fades).

findings.title: AnimationGroup choreographs multi-animation blending with layer blending modes
findings.evidence: keyframes.js/src/animation/group.ts:37-135 (AnimationGroup class); group.ts:198-289 (transformFramesGrouped: zIndex sort, layer properties whitelist, replace/add/weighted blend); engine.ts:126-200 (Animation composition into group)
findings.rootCause: Dock today composites width/opacity via separate CSS transitions (GlassDock.vue, DockLayerGroup.vue) without a choreography primitive. Simultaneous but unsynchronized (width settles before opacity, or vice versa, leading to visible artifacts).
findings.proposal: Feed the dock's collapse↔expand animation through AnimationGroup: one animation for width, one for opacity (the shrink-before-fade desync). Group them with layer.properties whitelisting to filter keys per layer, .blendMode blend rules (replace width, add shadow alpha), and advanceTo(t) drives both frames off one rAF loop. The group zero-allocs on steady-state (D.W4 closes this), so the compositor is hot-path-safe.
findings.gate: proof:desync-closed — simultaneous width and opacity animations on dock collapse show zero frame-time delay in the property settle (both reach target within 1 frame of each other)

findings.title: Timeline + SmoothProgress enable scroll-driven and gesture-tracked animation
findings.evidence: keyframes.js/src/animation/timeline.ts:36-162 (Timeline abstract class, ScrollTimeline/ManualTimeline subclasses); smooth.ts:43-150 (SmoothProgress damped-follower); playback.ts:162-179 (.drive() Tickable loop)
findings.rootCause: Dock today has no gesture-tracking primitive for mid-flight interrupts or drag-follow patterns (e.g. swipe-to-expand, drag-to-collapse). Each interaction is a discrete animate-from-A-to-B sequence.
findings.proposal: Adopt Timeline for scroll-linked dock sidebar (if the design calls for scroll-to-expand) and SmoothProgress for live-target tracking on gesture (tap-and-hold, drag-while-animating). Both compose seamlessly with SpringProgress: the timeline/smooth output feeds target to the spring, producing iOS-grade follow-through. The RAFPlayback driver unifies the rAF lifecycle across all three.

findings.title: Spring presets: iOS-canonical (response, dampingFraction) surface with critical damping at ζ=1
findings.evidence: keyframes.js/src/animation/spring.ts:54-62 defaultSpringOptions { response: 0.5, dampingFraction: 0.86 }; docs/tranches/C/audit/animation/ios-dock-animation.md:125-144 (six iOS presets table); springTimingFunction.ts:14-38 (mirror options)
findings.rootCause: Glass-ui's dock has no unified spring parametrization — it locks into fixed durations and hand-tuned curves per interaction (hover, press, expand, collapse), making the iOS character feel fragmented.
findings.proposal: Define dock spring presets mapped to the iOS vocabulary: (1) .spring() default (response 0.55, ζ 0.825) for full-layer morphs; (2) .interactiveSpring() (0.15, 0.86) for magnification/gesture-tracking; (3) .smooth critically-damped (ζ=1, response 0.5) for no-overshoot settle (collapse, hide); (4) .snappy lightly-underdamped (0.5, 0.85) for icon press-back. Each preset cascades to both JS (SpringProgress.play) and CSS (springLinearStops → --spring-* token). The dock then uses one preset per interaction class, unifying the motion vocabulary.
findings.gate: proof:preset-unity — the dock's four interaction classes (expand, shrink, press, release) each employ the same spring preset as calls-to-play and as the CSS transition-timing-function (via linear() stops), measured via performance.now() and diffing the JS/CSS settle times (±30ms within-noise tolerance)

findings.title: Dynamic import boundary keeps value.js out of light consumers
findings.evidence: keyframes.js/src/animation/index.ts:1-138 (LIGHT barrel exports SpringProgress/springLinearStops/Timeline; HEAVY boundary `await loadAnimationEngine()` for Animation/AnimationGroup/CSS parser); index.ts:27-54 (no static import of value.js in LIGHT surface)
findings.rootCause: Glass-ui's dock would need to load AnimationGroup + WAAPI delegation, which pulls value.js into the static graph. Today the dock avoids the engine (using plain CSS), so it stays light.
findings.proposal: Spring physics (SpringProgress) and spring-stop emission (springLinearStops) sit on the LIGHT static surface — zero value.js edge. AnimationGroup + Animation live behind the dynamic `await loadAnimationEngine()` boundary. A dock using springs needs no engine load unless it demands live CSS parsing (fromString keyframes) — the group can compose hand-rolled Animation-compatible frame arrays. If the dock stays hand-written (no from-string), the LIGHT surface alone (springs + morph + timeline) suffices, keeping value.js out of the critical path. If the dock needs CSS parsing, the load is explicit and one-time.
findings.gate: proof:boundary — measure static graph: a glass-ui dock consumer importing @mkbabb/glass-ui + DocSpringAnimator (hypothetical dock driver using SpringProgress but NO fromString) has ZERO value.js in bundled static graph (webpack --analyze / esbuild --metafile)

findings.title: AnimationGroup D.W4 closes per-frame allocations in the compositor hot loop
findings.evidence: keyframes.js/docs/tranches/D/D.md:215-232 (inv θ gate `proof:zero-alloc`); docs/tranches/D/waves/D.W4.md:27-61 (D-1 transposition: hoist _groupedValues buffer, inline properties.has whitelist)
findings.rootCause: AnimationGroup today allocates fresh groupedValues object + filteredValues per entry per frame when layer.properties whitelist is set (group.ts:199-228). The class declares zero-alloc but violates it in the sole hot loop.
findings.proposal: D.W4 (landing in the stacked major) hoists groupedValues to an instance _grouped buffer, clears in place each frame, and inlines the whitelist check in the three blend arms. No behavior change; only the allocation vanishes. This is load-bearing for dock: a dock compositing 2–4 animations simultaneously (width + opacity + shadow-blur + corner-radius) can sustain 60fps without heap growth. The gate is a NEW bench/zero-alloc.bench.ts proof that steady-state ≥120 frames allocate 0 bytes/frame.
findings.gate: proof:zero-alloc (D.W4 deliverable)

findings.title: Shrink-before-fade desync: CSS transitions diverge in time-compression and curve, AnimationGroup unifies
findings.evidence: glass-ui/src/components/custom/dock/GlassDock.vue:150-170 (the two transition declarations: width + opacity, separate duration/timing-function); useLayerTransition.ts:156-184 (FLIP fallback re-pins old size, animates to new; opacity crossfade is separate, uncoordinated); docs/tranches/C/audit/animation/ios-dock-animation.md:147-200 (Part II.1–2 documents the frozen spring 3× compressed, native VT swaps curve)
findings.rootCause: Width animation today is either (a) CSS transition with --spring-snappy (response 0.5, ζ 0.85) time-compressed 3× from physics into a fixed 300ms, or (b) View-Transition morphing with --ease-apple-spring (a different cubic-bezier hand-tuned for the VT path). Opacity is a separate CSS transition at a different rate. The two properties settle at different times, creating the visible frame where the dock is narrow but still showing the expanded content (or vice versa on close).
findings.proposal: Adopt AnimationGroup with two child animations: (1) width/height keyframes eased by springTimingFunction(response 0.5, ζ 0.86); (2) opacity keyframes eased by the same spring. Both animate on the same rAF loop via advanceTo(t), settling in lockstep. On the WAAPI path (if View-Transition is used), thread the spring's .css linear() stops into the CSS transition-timing-function so the compositor runs the same curve. The root cause is time-divergence; the fix is one authority (the spring) and one rAF driver (AnimationGroup) or one CSS declaration (the linear() stops).
findings.gate: proof:desync-closed (see KF-ANIMATION-GROUP-COMPOSITOR)

deferredItems.item: Gesture-driven drag-to-expand (iOS-like pan tracking)
deferredItems.source: keyframes.js audit findings (new, not in D ledger)
deferredItems.why: SmoothProgress and SpringProgress support live-target update (setTarget on each gesture frame), enabling true gesture tracking. This is a future glass-ui UX pattern, not a keyframes engine gap. The engine is ready; the dock design must call for it.

risks: Adopting AnimationGroup introduces a new orchestration primitive; dock call sites must coordinate width+opacity into one group rather than two independent CSS transitions. This is a refactor surface, not an engine risk.

SpringProgress settles asynchronously (typically 200–500ms depending on preset); if the dock fires visual transitions faster than settle (e.g. rapid collapse/expand), the group must handle interrupted animations. RAFPlayback.drive() already supports this (idempotent re-arm on target change); verify no stale rAF handles leak.

View-Transition morphing is a separate path from rAF; threading springLinearStops() into the CSS transition requires the dock to choose one authority (spring curve) + one fallback (CSS twin). Verify that the .css property survives transition-timing-function and does not get re-computed by the browser.
Zero-alloc group (D.W4) ships in the stacked major; dock consumers must update to the new major to access the allocation-free path. This is a version-boundary dependency, not a runtime risk.

findings.area: keyframes.js D-tranche DEMOS/REVIEWS — iOS-smooth motion recipes audit (READ-ONLY)
findings.summary: Audited keyframes.js D-tranche demo files and spring physics implementations to extract iOS-smooth motion recipes proven in testing. The canonical motion recipes are implemented via SpringProgress (analytic spring solver with iOS SwiftUI-canonical surface) and springTimingFunction sampling. Four preset spring curves are demonstrated: smooth (response 0.5s, dampingFraction 0.86 — critically-ish damped, no ringing); snappy (0.35s, 0.65 — quick with overshoot); bouncy (0.5s, 0.45 — pronounced overshoot, playful); gentle (0.7s, 1.0 — critically damped, slow). Stagger is achieved via per-frame tickDt integration with shared RAFPlayback clock, enabling phase-aligned animations across multiple children. Simultaneous morph+fade uses ElementMorph with spring timing functions plus parallel opacity animations. The demo's easing showcase (useEasingDemo) and spring comparison (useSpringDemo) provide proven patterns for dock motion: 60fps frame stepping (FRAME_MS = 1000/60), settle thresholds at 1e-4, and deterministic flush ordering on array watchers for stale-frame prevention.

findings.title: Spring Physics Surface — iOS SwiftUI-Canonical (response, dampingFraction)

findings.title: Spring Timing — Underdamped (ζ<1) Overshoot Pattern
findings.evidence: src/animation/spring.ts:62-88 (underdamped solver); test/spring.test.ts:62-76 (overshoot >1.05 for ζ=0.4); demo/spring/springPresets.ts:30-35 (bouncy: ζ=0.45 with ~20% overshoot)

findings.proposal: For dock panel expansion with playful feel: use springTimingFunction({response: 0.5, dampingFraction: 0.45}) to sample the spring ODE into a TimingFunction. The sampled curve will naturally overshoot beyond 100%, creating the iOS-signature 'snap' before settling. Feed this into ElementMorph or CSSKeyframesAnimation.timingFunction for the height/width morph.

findings.title: Critically Damped (ζ=1) No-Overshoot Pattern

findings.title: Stagger via Shared Clock + Deterministic Frame Integration
findings.evidence: demo/spring/useSpringDemo.ts:127-155 (shared RAFPlayback.loop(frame) drives 4 preset trackers simultaneously with single DOMHighResTimeStamp dt); demo/easing/useEasingDemo.ts:137-150 (linear phase sweep through alternate-direction keyframes, no magic dt seed)

Each tracker maintains its own `elapsed` time offset from target re-seat, enabling phase-aligned motion without explicit delay values.
findings.proposal: For dock panel stagger (items opening in sequence but smooth): Do NOT use CSS delay; instead drive all panels' morphs via one shared RAFPlayback, with each panel's spring.target set at offset frame counts (panel 0 target→1 at frame 0, panel 1 at frame 3, panel 2 at frame 6, etc.). The shared clock ensures they all settle together within their respective phases. Alternatively, use CSS stagger ONLY if pre-computing the exact settle time per damping fraction (settles in ~4×response typically).

findings.title: Simultaneous Morph + Fade Pattern — ElementMorph + Opacity
findings.evidence: src/animation/morph.ts (ElementMorph: scale + translate transforms); src/animation/animations.ts:5-22 (fadeIn: opacity 0→1); demo/playground/usePlaygroundAnimations.ts:19-24 (fadeIn 2000ms + rotation simultaneously)

findings.proposal: For dock panel appearance: Use AnimationGroup with two child animations: (1) ElementMorph(from: {x, y, width, height}, to: {x, y, width, height}, timingFunction: springTimingFunction({response: 0.5, dampingFraction: 0.86}), duration: 400), (2) CSSKeyframesAnimation({opacity: 0}→{opacity: 1}, same timingFunction, same duration). findings.title: Frame Integration Cadence — 60fps tickDt(ms) with Settle Thresholds
findings.evidence: demo/spring/useSpringDemo.ts:31-32 (SETTLE = 1e-4, SAMPLER_DURATION = 1400); test/spring.test.ts:5 (FRAME_MS = 1000/60 ≈ 16.667ms canonical step)

findings.proposal: For glass-ui dock: drive spring morphs with 60fps requestAnimationFrame, calling spring.tickDt(dt) with dt from performance.now(). Set settleThreshold: 1e-4 (default) for visual imperceptibility. For response 0.5s with smooth damping (0.86), the animation settles in ~800-1000ms; for snappy (0.35s, 0.65), ~500-700ms. Use spring.settled boolean to auto-stop the rAF loop (no memory leak, immediate when physics signal complete).

findings.title: Deterministic Flush Ordering — Array-Watch Post-Flush for Stale-Frame Prevention
findings.evidence: docs/tranches/D/wf-review.mjs:51 (D.W3.S4 — 'deterministic flush so a stale frame array can't paint'); demo/spring/useSpringDemo.ts:201 (watch([response, dampingFraction], rebuildLiveSpring) with no explicit flush param, relying on post-flush implicit ordering)
findings.rootCause: Vue array mutations in watch can race with template renders if the watch fires during setup. Explicit flush:'post' ensures the watcher runs AFTER the component renders, preventing a stale frame array from painting mid-morph.
findings.proposal: For dock panel expand/collapse: if using Vue computed frames or a reactive frame buffer, guard with `watch(frameArray, () => { ... }, { flush: 'post' })` to ensure the buffer is complete before any template re-render consumes it. This prevents a race where the buffer is half-written during render, causing a glitch or dropped frame.

findings.title: Spring Preset Defaults — Smooth (0.86) as iOS Standard

Use springTimingFunction({response: 0.5, dampingFraction: 0.86}) and feed the `.css` property to the animation's timingFunction in CSS. findings.title: Live Target Re-Seat — Continuous Velocity Preservation Across Interrupts

findings.area: glass-ui dock motion orchestration
findings.summary: The glass-ui dock's motion logic is orchestrated through a stratified, CSS-driven architecture rather than keyframes.js. The FLIP (First, Last, Invert, Play) composable `useLayerTransition` coordinates two levels of layer swaps: the outer collapsed↔expanded pair (GlassDock's `.dock-layers` container) and the inner DockLayerGroup stack. Both use the same motion primitive and share a forked path: native View-Transitions (browser-owned) or a CSS-interpolated FLIP fallback. The "dock shrinks first, items fade later" sequencing is enforced purely in CSS: the container's `width` animates via `--dock-motion-resize` while child opacity rides the SAME duration + spring curve (lockstep), with delayed `visibility: hidden` transitions holding leaving layers painted through the opacity fade. The ordering is geometric (grid + absolute positioning), not JS orchestration. No keyframes.js is involved; CSS `transition` primitives and the `startViewTransition()` API own all motion.

findings.title: Two-level FLIP layer orchestration with forked native/fallback paths
findings.evidence: useLayerTransition.ts:49-202 (both GlassDock.vue:206-210 for outer pair + DockLayerGroup.vue:56-60 for inner stack); the composable watches activeLayer and forks on `document.startViewTransition` support
findings.rootCause: Layer swaps (collapsed↔expanded, layer-to-layer) require size morphs that CSS `width: auto` cannot interpolate. FLIP solves this by measuring before/after sizes and pinning to pixel values for animation.
findings.proposal: The current architecture is idiomatic. Both layers use the same composable with axis awareness (horizontal vs vertical), eliminating duplication. The forking is clean: native path uses `startViewTransition(() => swap())` for browser-native morph; fallback runs FLIP verbatim (measure→pin→swap→measure→re-pin→animate→cleanup). Proposal: document the generation/morphGeneration guard pattern (lines 146-154 in GlassDock.vue) as the canonical concurrency control for >=2-dock rapid re-triggers (collapses/expands superseding each other). No code change needed; this is load-bearing.

findings.title: CSS lockstep opacity + delayed visibility for layer crossfade-with-holdup

AU.W2 locked the fade to the morph duration so both settle in sync, with the visibility transition holding a leaving layer painted (not hidden) for the full opacity duration.
findings.proposal: The lockstep is correct and is the idiomatic fix. Proposal: no change. The visibility delayed-clear (0s delay on active, var(--duration-normal) delay on inactive) is the pattern that keeps leaving layers answerable to `elementFromPoint()` during the crossfade, preventing hit-test misses. This is a CSS-only solution and lives correctly here.

findings.title: Container resize (width) is FLIP-driven, not inline-pinned; children fade lockstep

Document this in motion.md as the canonical concurrency control for multi-property transitions with mixed durations. The RESIZE_MORPH_PROPS Set (line 262) filters onDockTransitionDone to only width/height/padding/transform, ignoring the faster surface properties.

findings.title: No keyframes.js involvement; CSS spring curve + View-Transitions own all motion
findings.evidence: composables/motion/motion.ts exports useSpring/useAnimatedNumber but zero imports in dock components. dock.css:26 defines --dock-motion-resize: var(--duration-normal) var(--dock-resize-spring), where --dock-resize-spring is --spring-snappy (a CSS linear() curve from tokens.css). useViewTransition.ts:80-103 runs the browser's startViewTransition for the native path, falling back to FLIP on non-supporting engines.

If a consumer wants to retune the spring for their dock variant, they override `--dock-resize-spring` or `--dock-motion-resize` at the `.glass-dock` level. The pattern is Tailwind-first and token-native, avoiding any keyframes.js carrying cost.

findings.title: Pseudo-element tree and group naming strategy correctly wired
findings.evidence: src/styles/view-transition.css:37-65 defines group recipes for both `.gl-list-item` (generic list re-rank) and `.gl-dock-layer` (dock-specific); uses `:only-child` pseudo for add/remove members (::view-transition-new/:only-child slides in, ::view-transition-old/:only-child slides out); per-instance `view-transition-name` minted from Vue `useId()` (GlassDock.vue:226, sanitized to remove non-alphanumeric chars per the CSS IDENT grammar)
findings.rootCause: The View Transitions API synthesizes a pseudo-element tree when `startViewTransition` runs: `::view-transition > ::view-transition-group(name) > ::view-transition-image-pair > [::view-transition-old, ::view-transition-new]`. Naming collisions (>1 element per name per state) silently skip the transition. Glass-ui avoids this via `useId()` collision-free naming (app-scoped, survives lazy/eager module-graph copies).
findings.proposal: Current approach is optimal: (1) the `.gl-list-item` + `.gl-dock-layer` group recipes cluster shared animation rules (duration + timing-function from tokens, no hardcoded values); (2) `view-transition-class` binds the recipe (abstraction boundary between CSS authoring and JS naming); (3) `:only-child` slide keyframes (in/out) apply only to added/removed members, preserving cross-fade for re-ordered members. No changes needed. iOS Safari (15+) lacks VT support; the FLIP fallback is the live path on iOS, and it's branch-less (no conditional animation code).

findings.title: Reduced-motion compliance correctly gates all VT animations
findings.evidence: src/styles/view-transition.css:27-33 gates all `::view-transition-*` pseudo animations to `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { animation: none !important; }`. The native swap still runs (state mutates instantly), motion simply disables. FLIP fallback (useLayerTransition.ts lines 135-185) is branch-less (motion disabled is a no-op transition, not a code fork).
findings.rootCause: The View Transitions API respects the user's motion preference via the browser's prefers-reduced-motion match. Glass-ui correctly leverages this by gating VT group animations, not the transition itself. On iOS (Safari 15+), the FLIP fallback runs instead, and CSS transitions honor prefers-reduced-motion natively (no explicit gate needed in TS).
findings.proposal: Current implementation is correct-at-HEAD. Measurement point (optional): on macOS Safari 15+ where both engines might coexist, verify the browser's prefers-reduced-motion gate is respected (the CSS rule is valid for both Apple platforms). No code changes needed.

findings.title: FLIP fallback relationship: VT eliminates manual measure/pin/animate cycle, FLIP preserved as feature-detected fallback
findings.evidence: src/components/custom/dock/composables/useLayerTransition.ts:31-48 documents the fork: VT path (lines 115-132) wraps the swap in `startViewTransition`, ZERO `getBoundingClientRect` calls; FLIP fallback (lines 135-185) runs verbatim 6-step cycle (capture → pin → swap → nextTick measure → re-pin → animate). Lines 56-57 fork once at composable construction (VT is stable engine capability, not per-swap condition).
findings.rootCause: FLIP (First-Last-Invert-Play) is a performance technique: (1) capture initial layout (First), (2) apply final classes (Last), (3) invert with transforms to rewind visually (Invert), (4) animate to final state (Play). It trades CPU measurement cost upfront for GPU-cheap compositor animations. VT replaces steps 1, 3, 4: the browser snapshots (First, Last), constructs the pseudo-element tree automatically (Invert), and runs the animation (Play). Step 2 (the DOM swap) still happens synchronously inside the callback.
findings.proposal: Current approach is SOTA-idiomatic: (1) VT eliminates layout thrashing by deferring measurement to the browser's snapshot engine (no rAF loops, no forced reflow); (2) FLIP fallback is the sole non-VT path, feature-detected, not aliased (clean break per precept 1); (3) the timing curve is unified (one-source-one-engine contract). For iOS smoothness: iOS Safari 15+ does NOT support View Transitions, so the FLIP fallback is the live path on iPad/iPhone. The spring curve (linear()) is GPU-efficient and settles without overshoot, delivering 60fps on modern iOS devices. No changes needed.

findings.title: Morph-generation concurrency guard prevents skip-fast-forward + stale-clear on rapid A→B→A re-triggers
findings.evidence: src/components/custom/dock/GlassDock.vue:146-154 (morphGeneration counter), 269-287 (markTransitioning bumps generation, timer fallback captures it), 279-287 (onDockTransitionDone compares event's generation to current, no-ops if stale). Test: src/components/custom/dock/__tests__/GlassDock.motion-parity.test.ts lines 61-83 (rapid A→B→A faster than one morph completes, flag stays true until LAST morph resolves; stale events are ignored).
findings.rootCause: A ≥2-dock rapid expand→collapse→expand scenario can fire transitionend events out of order. Without a generation guard, a stale A→B `transitionend` (finishing late) could clear `isTransitioning` while the live B→A morph is still in flight, causing visible jank. The guard captures the generation counter live at each morph start, so stale events no-op.
findings.proposal: Current guard is correct-at-HEAD per the proof:dock-motion-parity gate. For iOS: the FLIP fallback's timeout-based cleanup (useLayerTransition.ts:180-184) also captures a transitionId and no-ops if superseded. The contracts are dual-redundant: static gate (proof script) + runtime test. No changes needed.

findings.title: Cross-document View Transitions not applicable to dock morph; same-document sufficient
findings.evidence: src/composables/motion/useViewTransition.ts is same-document only (calls `document.startViewTransition`). Cross-document VT (Chrome 126+) requires `@view-transition { navigation: auto; }` in CSS and is triggered on same-origin navigation automatically—the dock morph is a single-document state swap, not a page load.
findings.rootCause: Cross-document VT is designed for multi-page apps (SPA page transitions). The dock is a component-local state machine (expanded ↔ collapsed within one document). Same-document is the correct scope.
findings.proposal: No action needed. If a future slides deck consumer needs page-transition VT between briefing slides (a different use case from dock), that would require the @view-transition CSS rule and automatic navigation triggering. The dock motion is wholly within same-document scope.

findings.title: iOS smoothness: spring curve is correct, but verify device-specific frame metrics
findings.evidence: `--spring-snappy` is a 45-point `linear()` function (tokens.css:1186) encoding settling spring physics: underdamped (overshoot absorbed), ~0.3s nominal duration. Composable fork (useLayerTransition.ts:56-57) detects VT once, so on iOS (no VT) the FLIP path always runs. The spring curve drives the CSS transition in the FLIP path (dock.css:26: `--dock-motion-resize: var(--duration-normal) var(--dock-resize-spring)`).
findings.rootCause: iOS Safari 15+ (the minimum iOS WKWebView version on iPad/iPhone) does NOT support the View Transitions API (Baseline coverage is Chromium 111+, macOS Safari 17.2+). The dock morph on iOS is always the FLIP fallback. The spring curve is GPU-efficient (compositor-only, no JS-driven rAF). Whether the morph FEELS 'iOS-smooth' depends on device frame-rate match: 60fps (most iPhones, iPads) or 120fps (Pro models). The curve itself is a generic settling spring, not iOS-specific.
findings.proposal: To achieve 'iOS-smooth' feel: (1) measure the actual frame cadence on target iOS devices (use iOS Profiler or Safari DevTools remote inspect). (2) Confirm the spring curve's perceived smoothness at device-native fps (60 vs 120). (3) If needed, tune `--spring-snappy`'s damping coefficient (the `linear()` points encode (response, damping); currently ~0.86 damping, close to iOS canonical). (4) Consider adopting an `@media (update: fast)` / `@media (update: slow)` gate if 60fps devices feel jank (though on modern iOS, 60fps should be solid). Current code is frame-rate-agnostic; the spring curve is stable. No immediate change required—verification step only.

findings.title: Directional slide animation: VT group :only-child keyframes enable directional hint (future feature, not required)
findings.evidence: src/styles/view-transition.css:44-45 define `::view-transition-new(.gl-list-item):only-child { animation-name: gl-vt-slide-in; }` and `::view-transition-old(.gl-list-item):only-child { animation-name: gl-vt-slide-out; }` with `--vt-rise: 8px` offset. These animate only added/removed list members, not re-ordered ones. The dock layer recipe (.gl-dock-layer) does NOT override these; it uses the default cross-fade.
findings.rootCause: The `:only-child` trick (from Chrome's View Transitions group guide) differentiates add/remove (slide) from re-order (cross-fade). The dock layer-swap is logically an element replace (old pane → new pane), so a slide would be semantically correct. Currently the dock inherits the default cross-fade. A future refinement (F14, BOOKED in AT.W1b §4) could add directional awareness: dock collapsed→expanded might slide in from the left, expanded→collapsed slide out to the left (axis-aware, matching the dock's expansion direction).
findings.proposal: BOOK for future. Do NOT land now: (1) no firm iOS consumer yet (speedtest deck is the consumer, not a dock-motion user); (2) directional VT requires JS to tag each pane with `view-transition-name` dynamically (the current implementation is static per container); (3) the added visual polish (slide vs fade) is optional, not load-bearing. Land this alongside a real directional-morph consumer (a slide deck with forward/back navigation, or an iOS-style sheet dismiss). Current cross-fade is correct-at-HEAD.

findings.title: Paint timing and rendering: VT snapshot → pseudo-element tree → CSS animation is compositor-safe
findings.evidence: src/styles/view-transition.css:68 sets `::view-transition { pointer-events: none; }` to keep the live UI interactive during the snapshot animation. The FLIP fallback uses only `transform` + `opacity` on the container (height/width on the dimension property, both compositor-friendly in modern engines). No layout-triggering properties on the animated elements.
findings.rootCause: The View Transitions API's snapshot pipeline: (1) `startViewTransition` wraps the callback, (2) browser pauses rendering, (3) takes a screenshot of old state, (4) runs the callback (DOM swap happens here, no rendering), (5) takes a screenshot of new state, (6) constructs the pseudo-element tree with both snapshots, (7) animates the pseudo-layer via CSS (the old snapshot fades out, new snapshot fades in). This is GPU-driven—no forced reflows, no JS-driven rAF loops. The FLIP path uses CSS `transition` on box properties, also GPU-friendly (transform only, no expensive properties like `width` animated directly—it's pinned before/after animation).
findings.proposal: Current implementation is optimal. No changes needed. For iOS: the FLIP fallback's paint cost is negligible (one transition per state change, cached metrics pre-computed). Frame rate stability is the verification step (iOS Profiler, measure janky frames during rapid dock expand/collapse cycles).

findings.title: Safari/iOS support path: VT not available on iOS 15, FLIP fallback is the live engine
findings.evidence: src/composables/motion/useViewTransition.ts:58-62 feature-detect `document.startViewTransition` and return `{ transitioned: false }` if absent, triggering the instant fallback (mutate runs synchronously, no animation). useLayerTransition.ts:56-57 hard-forks on VT support at construction time; on iOS (no VT), the FLIP path always runs. src/components/custom/dock/GlassDock.vue:221-222 sets `supportsVT` computed once, conditionally applies `view-transition-*` CSS only on supporting engines.
findings.rootCause: iOS Safari 15.x (the minimum WebKit version on iPad/iPhone OS 15–17) does NOT support the View Transitions API. The spec is Baseline Widely (Chromium 111+, desktop Safari 17.2+, but NOT mobile Safari yet). The dock implementation correctly degrades: on iOS, `startViewTransition` is undefined, the feature-detect returns false, and the FLIP fallback runs (CSS transitions on the container's size). The UX is smooth (spring curve, 60fps cap on devices), but motion-wise it's a state-synchronous size-morph, not a snapshot-based animation.
findings.proposal: No action needed—the implementation is already future-proof. When iOS Safari (likely iOS 19+) gains VT support, the code will automatically activate the native path (no code change required, feature-detect will return true). Current baseline is sound: FLIP fallback is production-ready on iOS, VT is a performance enhancement on browsers that support it.

risks: Timing divergence on older browsers: if FLIP fallback's CSS spring curve ever drifts from `--dock-resize-spring` definition (e.g., via token rename), the static gate proof:dock-motion-parity will catch it (fail-closed), but consumers on older browsers may see stale easing. Mitigation: the gate is run on every CI build; the rename table in MIGRATION.md documents any token changes.

iOS device heterogeneity: 60fps vs 120fps-capable devices may perceive the spring curve differently (settling overshoots on 120fps feel crisper). No measurement baseline exists yet. Mitigation: launch with the current snappy spring (0.86 damping); collect iOS Profiler metrics post-deploy to decide if tuning is needed. The linear() encoding is flexible and can be re-fit without code changes.

Future cross-document VT adoption: if slides deck (SL) transitions between briefing decks via page navigation, both pages must opt-in to `@view-transition { navigation: auto; }` in CSS. If one page is legacy (pre-AQ.W5), the other page's VT will silently not animate. Mitigation: document the CSS rule in slides' design system docs; require it in any page that participates in cross-document transitions.

Rapid re-trigger concurrency: although the morphGeneration guard prevents skip-fast-forward + stale-clear, a user who mash-toggles the dock faster than one morph completes will see queued morphs. The flag stays true (correct) but the user might perceive visual lag if the morph duration is intentionally long (current 0.3s is snappy). Mitigation: the visual queue is functional (no jank); if UX research shows users dislike queueing, add a debounce or gesture-cancel policy (not a motion issue, a UX choice).

findings.area: glass-ui dock collapse/expand size animations and entry-exit primitives
findings.summary: Researched modern CSS size-animation primitives and found that glass-ui's dock component relies on JS-based FLIP (First, Last, Invert, Play) width measurement to animate between collapsed/expanded states. The platform now natively supports three modern features: (1) `@starting-style` with `transition-behavior:allow-discrete` for discrete property animations (already adopted in animations.css for top-layer popovers), (2) `interpolate-size:allow-keywords` paired with CSS transitions to animate to/from `auto` dimensions without JS measurement, and (3) `transition-behavior:allow-discrete` on `overlay` and `display` properties for smooth entry/exit without visibility jitter. The dock's current "shrink-before-fade" lag (AU.W2 fixes) stems from the layer opacity crossfade running on `--dock-motion-resize` (0.3s spring) while the container size animates via JS FLIP measurement (same timing but synchronized separately). A pure-CSS path using modern size-animation primitives would eliminate JS height/width measurement entirely and provide native entry/exit for vertically-collapsing content via `interpolate-size` and `calc-size(auto)` instead of fixed pixel pinning in useLayerTransition.

findings.title: Dock width animation relies on JS-based FLIP measurement with manual size pinning
findings.evidence: /Users/mkbabb/Programming/glass-ui/src/components/custom/dock/composables/useLayerTransition.ts:49-202, specifically lines 140-170 (fallback path: pin size, swap layer classes, measure new size, re-pin to old, then animate via CSS transition)
findings.rootCause: CSS does not natively interpolate `width:auto` to fixed pixel values, so the FLIP strategy captures the old size (line 140: `const fromSize = getSize(el)`), pins the element inline (line 143: `setDim(el, '${fromSize}px')`), swaps the DOM layer (lines 145-147), measures the new natural size (line 157: `const toSize = getSize(el)`), re-pins to old (line 160: `setDim(el, '${fromSize}px')`), then animates to new via CSS transition (line 169: `setDim(el, '${toSize}px')`)
findings.proposal: Adopt `interpolate-size:allow-keywords` on `.dock-layers` to enable smooth CSS transitions from current width to `width:auto` (or vice versa) WITHOUT manual getBoundingClientRect() calls. Replace the JS FLIP measurement loop with: (1) set `interpolate-size:allow-keywords` base rule on the container, (2) use CSS transitions to `width:auto` on active layer swap, (3) let the browser measure and interpolate natively. This eliminates the getBoundingClientRect burden (lines 62, 140, 157), the inline style pinning dance (lines 143, 160, 169), and the nextTick/offsetWidth reflow choreography (lines 150-162, 167). The View-Transitions native path (lines 121-133) already escapes this overhead entirely; the fallback becomes equally modern.

findings.title: @starting-style + transition-behavior:allow-discrete pattern already exists for top-layer; extend to dock size transitions
findings.evidence: /Users/mkbabb/Programming/glass-ui/src/styles/animations.css:300-366 (.glass-top-layer pattern with @starting-style, transition-behavior:allow-discrete, and overlay property animation)
findings.rootCause: The dock layer crossfade (dock.css:424-450) uses `visibility` + `opacity` transitions but the `visibility` change rides on a delayed 0s transition (line 428: `visibility 0s linear var(--duration-normal)`). This discrete property flip happens AFTER the opacity fade completes, preventing synchronized entry/exit. The top-layer grammar in animations.css (line 335) shows the correct pattern: `transition-behavior:allow-discrete` on the transition list allows `display` and `overlay` to be included in the same transition chain as continuous properties like `opacity`.
findings.proposal: Apply the top-layer entry-exit recipe to dock layer pairs: (1) add `transition-behavior:allow-discrete` to `.dock-layer` and `.dock-layer-item-host` transition declarations (dock.css:426-429, 447-449), (2) nest `@starting-style` rules inside `.dock-layer.layer-active` and `.dock-layer-item-host.is-active` to define the entry starting-state (opacity:0, visibility:hidden before the transition), (3) keep `visibility` on the main transition list but pair it with `allow-discrete` so it flips at 0% on entry and 100% on exit (synchronized with opacity fade, not deferred). This makes the entry/exit timing isomorphic to the .glass-top-layer contract — same visibility-grip vocabulary, same discrete-property choreography.

findings.title: Vertical dock rail with auto-height layout (overflow:wrap, wrap content) has no smooth size animation
findings.evidence: /Users/mkbabb/Programming/glass-ui/src/styles/dock.css:201-223 (vertical rail with flex-direction:column, `height:auto`, no height pinning or animation), GlassDock.vue:135 (alwaysExpanded forced to true for vertical orientation, suppressing collapse/expand state machine), useLayerTransition.ts does not support vertical axis for the collapsed↔expanded pair (line 205: `outerLayerAxis` computed as `'horizontal'` always)
findings.rootCause: Vertical docks are always-expanded (GlassDock.vue:135), so the collapsed/expanded swap never fires. When content inside a vertical rail's layer wraps (overflow='wrap' on horizontal dock → dock-overflow-wrap class), the height becomes `auto` (dock.css:576-577) and the `.dock-layer-stack` height animates via transition (line 690: `transition: height var(--dock-motion-resize)`). However, the active layer's `height:auto` does not animate smoothly — it snaps from the old height to the new height, with opacity crossfading independently on `--dock-motion-resize` (creating lag if the layer swap triggers a height-measurement phase).
findings.proposal: Enable `interpolate-size:allow-keywords` on `.dock-layer-stack` (the height-animated grid container in `.dock-layer-group` contexts) so `height:auto` transitions smoothly. For vertical dock rails that might future-support collapse/expand: (1) lift the vertical-axis support in useLayerTransition (currently only horizontal; axis parameter exists but outerLayerAxis is hardcoded 'horizontal'), (2) apply `interpolate-size:allow-keywords` to the `.dock-layers` container when orientation='vertical', (3) pair with @starting-style to define the pre-swap height state so entry-exit is smooth. This future-proofs vertical collapse and fixes height-wrapping lag in horizontal docks with multi-line content.

findings.title: The AU.W2 'opacity-lockstep' fix synchronizes fade/morph timing but hides the root lag: missing entry-state definition
findings.evidence: /Users/mkbabb/Programming/glass-ui/src/styles/dock.css:416-450 (AU.W2 comment at line 416: 'the items appeared to lag the pill' — describes a 100ms-apart settle between the 0.2s fade and 0.3s morph before AU.W2). The fix locks both to `--dock-motion-resize` (0.3s spring) but the `.dock-layer:not(.layer-active)` rule (lines 431-436) has no @starting-style block defining opacity:0/visibility:hidden BEFORE the fade begins.
findings.rootCause: The dock layer swap is reactive (watch activeLayer in useLayerTransition), not entry-based. The old layer's opacity is already 0 and visibility:hidden in the DOM before the swap fires, so there is no entry-from state. The new layer flips to .layer-active (opacity:1, visibility:visible) with the transition already defined, but there is no @starting-style rule declaring 'start from opacity:0' — the browser infers starting-state from the old computed styles of the element, which may not exist or may be stale. Adding @starting-style rules ensures a consistent entry-state regardless of prior DOM state (e.g., if the layer was just inserted or swapped from `display:none`).
findings.proposal: Wrap @starting-style blocks inside `.dock-layer.layer-active` and `.dock-layer-item-host.is-active` rules (dock.css:438-450, similar nesting in the top-layer example at animations.css:340-348). Define starting opacity:0 and visibility:hidden (or the exiting-state values) inside @starting-style. This ensures that even if a layer is first-rendered or swapped from the DOM, the browser knows the precise entry-from state and animates smoothly without guessing. Pairs with allow-discrete to make visibility a first-class animated property, not a delayed side effect.

findings.title: Browser support for interpolate-size and transition-behavior:allow-discrete is Baseline 2024; safe to adopt
findings.evidence: WebFetch results: transition-behavior Baseline 2024 (Chrome 117+, Firefox 129+, Safari 17.4+, Opera 103+, mobile browsers 17.4+); @starting-style Baseline 2024 (same timeline); interpolate-size is similar Baseline timeline (drafts.csswg.org references it as part of CSS Sizing Module Level 4 with modern browser adoption)
findings.rootCause: glass-ui's minimum supported browser versions were historically tied to pre-2024 engines. The project's eslint + TypeScript + Vue 3 baseline already indicates modern language/runtime targets (ES2020+). Baseline 2024 features are safe to adopt now in 2026 for greenfield CSS animations.
findings.proposal: No blocking concerns. All three features (interpolate-size, transition-behavior:allow-discrete, @starting-style) shipped in Baseline 2024. Add a comment block in dock.css citing the Baseline 2024 timeline and referencing the spec sources (CSS Sizing-4 for interpolate-size, CSS Transitions-2 for transition-behavior, CSS Cascades-5 for @starting-style). No polyfill or fallback needed — non-supporting engines will see an instant (non-animated) state change, which is acceptable for a dock animation (users on legacy browsers don't expect motion anyway).

risks: Removing the JS FLIP measurement from useLayerTransition.ts requires careful testing on engines without View-Transitions support (still within scope, but fallback path changes from 'measure + pin + animate' to 'let browser measure via interpolate-size'). The getSize/setDim/clearDim methods can be deleted, but the transitionend handler + cleanup timer must stay to resolve the morph flag (isTransitioning).

Vertical dock support in useLayerTransition (the outer collapsed↔expanded pair) is untested in production — the current code hardcodes outerLayerAxis='horizontal' and alwaysExpanded forces vertical docks never to collapse. Enabling vertical axis requires careful motion testing and may expose edge cases in DockLayerGroup's vertical-axis support (which already exists but is internal).

The @starting-style + @supports(overlay:auto) recipe requires confirmation that no downstream CSS specificity fights occur. The .dock-layer rules live in a @layer components block (dock.css:8) and need to nest @starting-style correctly without scope leakage.

Adopting interpolate-size:allow-keywords changes the animation path from 'FLIP pins a fixed size' to 'browser measures intrinsic size via intrinsic-size() algorithm'. This may expose subtle layout shift bugs if a dock layer's natural size is data-driven (e.g., dynamic content, responsive breakpoints). Should add a regression test suite: dock with 10+ items, dock with 1 item, dock with very-long text, dock at breakpoint transitions.

findings.area: Spring physics, CSS linear() easing, iOS motion feel for dock collapse/expand + layer morph in glass-ui and slides deck
findings.summary: Glass-ui already achieves SOTA spring physics via keyframes.js's analytically-solved second-order damped harmonic oscillator (SpringProgress), paired with CSS linear() token generation (48-sample grid for 20%+ overshoot fidelity). Four iOS-canonical presets (smooth/snappy/bouncy/gentle) are source-of-truth in glass-ui/scripts/regen-spring-tokens.mjs. Dock collapse/expand currently uses snappy spring (response=0.35s, ζ=0.65, +6.8% overshoot) via --dock-resize-spring token. Layer morph and crossfade are already motion-locked per AU.W2 audit (both on --dock-motion-resize, snappy timing). Dock press micro-feedback uses bouncy (response=0.5s, ζ=0.45, +20.5% overshoot) on transform-only. All paths honor prefers-reduced-motion via unified withReducedMotion() gate. Proposal: no changes needed — existing parameters already deliver iOS-like critically-damped feel with appropriate spring-back; wire remaining consumers to PRM gate for accessibility.

findings.title: Single authoritative spring solver in keyframes.js
findings.evidence: /Users/mkbabb/Programming/keyframes.js/src/animation/spring.ts:82-408 (SpringProgress class with analytical second-order ODE solver); /Users/mkbabb/Programming/keyframes.js/src/animation/springLinearStops.ts:46-73 (CSS linear() generation); /Users/mkbabb/Programming/keyframes.js/src/animation/springTimingFunction.ts:65-120 (JS easing paired with CSS string)
findings.rootCause: Architecture separates physics (SpringProgress) from presentation (linear() stops vs JS easing function), ensuring one solver drives all motion across JS and CSS paths without duplication or drift.
findings.proposal: Status: ACHIEVED. No source-of-truth fragmentation. Glass-ui consumers import springLinearStops and springTimingFunction directly, or consume pre-generated --spring-* CSS tokens. All three paths (JS easing, CSS linear(), frame-by-frame playback) step the same solver with identical parameters.

findings.title: Dock collapse/expand morph uses iOS snappy preset
findings.evidence: /Users/mkbabb/Programming/glass-ui/src/styles/tokens.css:1266 (--dock-resize-spring: var(--spring-snappy)); /Users/mkbabb/Programming/glass-ui/src/styles/dock.css:20 (--dock-motion-resize uses --dock-resize-spring); /Users/mkbabb/Programming/glass-ui/scripts/regen-spring-tokens.mjs:38-42 (snappy preset: response=0.35s, ζ=0.65, +6.8% overshoot comment)
findings.rootCause: Glass-ui audit G-AJ retuned bouncy and snappy presets (AL.W9-γ retune, verified in regen script comments). Snappy delivers quick, crisp response with subtle spring-back ideal for dock resize; ζ=0.65 sits between iOS's 'smooth' (ζ=0.86, no overshoot) and 'bouncy' (ζ=0.45, 20%+ overshoot).
findings.proposal: KEEP as-is. The snappy preset (0.35s response, 0.65 damping) is iOS-canonical and already tuned. It produces ~6.8% overshoot, delivering the 'springy and iOS-like' tactile feel without being playful (bouncy) or stiff (smooth). This is the audited value per G-AJ.

findings.title: Layer crossfade + container morph locked on snappy timing (AU.W2 audit)

findings.area: Glass-UI Dock Animation Architecture & Compositor-Only Motion Discipline
findings.summary: The dock currently animates width/height directly via FLIP, which triggers layout recalculation—a jank risk on 60fps. Compositor-only properties (transform/opacity) run efficiently on the GPU without layout reflow. The codebase already employs transform-based patterns elsewhere (scroll-progress uses scaleX 0→1; press-feedback uses scale). The dock morph should migrate from width/height animation to a transform-scaleX-based container resize paired with children fade+scale stagger, creating an iOS-like orchestrated gesture where the pill morphing and content appearing read as one cohesive motion.

findings.title: Dock animates layout-triggering width/height properties directly
findings.evidence: /Users/mkbabb/Programming/glass-ui/src/styles/dock.css:382-386 (.dock-layers transition: width), :687-690 (.dock-layer-stack transition: width/height), :215-217 (vertical .glass-dock transitions height/width). /Users/mkbabb/Programming/glass-ui/src/components/custom/dock/composables/useLayerTransition.ts:59-62 (getSize reads width/height via getBoundingClientRect).
findings.rootCause: The FLIP mechanism measures natural size by reading width/height from getBoundingClientRect, then animates via inline style setProperty('width'/'height'). Width/height are layout-triggering properties that force full recalc. Each frame triggers reflow: measure → repin → animate → repeat.
findings.proposal: Replace width/height animation with a compositor-only `transform: scaleX()` morph on the `.dock-layers` container, paired with transform-origin logic. The FLIP sequence stays (measure natural width, pin, swap, measure new, animate), but the animation target becomes a scale factor derived from the width ratio, not width itself. This runs on the compositor without layout reflow. Pair with orchestrated children stagger: fade+scale opacity/transform on layer children on 40-60ms intervals to read as one iOS-gesture morphing the pill while content fades+scales in.
findings.gate: proof:dock-motion-parity (existing; gate already covers morph generation + transitionend semantics)

findings.title: Dock FLIP captures width but animates it; compositor-only scaleX is zero-jank alternative
findings.evidence: /Users/mkbabb/Programming/glass-ui/src/components/custom/dock/composables/useLayerTransition.ts:140,156-159 (captures fromSize via getSize(el) on width, then setDim(el, `${fromSize}px`) pins it). Line 169 setDim(el, `${toSize}px`) animates width. Web.dev: 'Restrict animations to `opacity` and `transform` to keep animations on the compositing stage of the rendering path.'
findings.rootCause: Width animates via CSS transition on a layout-triggering property. Each animation frame triggers: layout calc → paint → composite. Transform and opacity skip layout and paint, running compositor-only.
findings.proposal: Derive scaleX = toSize / fromSize. Pin container to fromSize width, swap layers, measure toSize. Animate via `transform: scaleX(${toSize / fromSize})` instead of width. Set `transform-origin: left 50%` to morph from the pill's left edge (or center for a centered morph—design choice). The layer children inside scale along with the container; add separate opacity/transform on each child to control entry stagger independently. This removes layout triggers entirely.

findings.title: Missing child stagger orchestration for zero-jank dock entry gesture
findings.evidence: /Users/mkbabb/Programming/glass-ui/src/styles/dock.css:424-429 (layer crossfade is opacity-only; no stagger). /Users/mkbabb/Programming/glass-ui/src/composables/motion/useStaggerReveal.ts demonstrates stagger pattern (staggerMs * idx offsets reveal). Dock has no equivalent per-child stagger on layer swap.
findings.rootCause: The dock layer pair crossfades synchronously on `--dock-motion-resize` (0.3s), but there is no children stagger within the active layer. Individual items (DockIconButton, DockTabButton) appear all-at-once when the layer becomes active. This reads as items popping in, not morphing through.
findings.proposal: Add a `--dock-stagger-delay` CSS variable (default 40-50ms per child). On layer activation (`.layer-active` or `.is-active` state), each child gets a staggered `animation-delay: calc(var(--dock-stagger-index) * var(--dock-stagger-delay))`. Children inside `.dock-layer--full` are indexed 0,1,2,... via `:nth-child()` or explicit `data-index`. Each child fades+scales: `opacity: 0 → 1` and `transform: scale(0.9) translateY(-4px) → scale(1) translateY(0)` on a 0.2s ease, offsetted by index. Orchestrated with the container scaleX morph creates the iOS gesture feel—pill morphs while content staggeres in.

findings.title: View Transition path already ships; FLIP fallback can be optimized to compositor-safe transform
findings.evidence: /Users/mkbabb/Programming/glass-ui/src/components/custom/dock/GlassDock.vue:221-230 (View Transition fork: `startViewTransition` in document). /Users/mkbabb/Programming/glass-ui/src/components/custom/dock/composables/useLayerTransition.ts:121-133 (native VT path owns size morph). Lines 135-186 (FLIP fallback—the one using width animation).
findings.rootCause: View Transitions (native path, ~95% browsers) skip the FLIP fallback and morph size natively. The FLIP code path fires only on engines without startViewTransition support (legacy). Width animation only matters in fallback, which is narrow in scope, but it's still present.
findings.proposal: The native VT path needs no change (browser owns the morph). The FLIP fallback should migrate width → scaleX for consistency and insurance: if a browser has VT but it glitches, fallback is still zero-jank. Refactor useLayerTransition setDim/clearDim to scaleX-based math: store original width on pin, derive scale ratio on new measurement, animate via transform scaleX. This decouples size animation from layout entirely.

findings.title: RESIZE_MORPH_PROPS includes both layout (width/height) and safe (padding/transform) triggers
findings.evidence: /Users/mkbabb/Programming/glass-ui/src/components/custom/dock/GlassDock.vue:262 (RESIZE_MORPH_PROPS = new Set(['width', 'height', 'padding', 'transform'])). Lines 283-287 (onDockTransitionDone checks if propertyName in this set to resolve isTransitioning).
findings.rootCause: Padding is a compound property that can trigger layout (if it changes intrinsic size). By including it in RESIZE_MORPH_PROPS, the dock waits for the longest transition of any of these four. If transform finishes first (likely, since it's compositor-only), the flag could theoretically clear early (though padding's delay likely keeps the flag set longer).
findings.proposal: Separate RESIZE_MORPH_PROPS into two sets: LAYOUT_PROPS (width, height, padding) and COMPOSITOR_PROPS (transform). The morph resolves when LAYOUT_PROPS complete (if animating them) OR when the longest overall transition completes. Once migrated to scaleX, LAYOUT_PROPS is empty and only transform+opacity matter—purely compositor. This tightens the semantics and future-proofs for when width/height animations are gone.

risks: Migrating FLIP from width to scaleX changes the DOM measurement contract: derived scale from ratio (toSize / fromSize) must be pixel-perfect or drift occurs. Test on edge cases: single-item layers, max-width overflows, density changes. Stagger delay indexing requires children DOM to be stable; if children reorder mid-transition, stagger indices become stale—guard with stable keys.

ScaleX morph origin must match design intent: left-aligned morph pulls from the left edge (common for docks), centered pulls from middle. If changed later, children stagger + container scale can read as misaligned. Document the choice and make it a consumer-overridable token.

Stagger on layer children via :nth-child() CSS is fragile if slot markup changes (e.g., adding a separator or spacer). Use a more explicit indexing scheme: data-index on each child or rely on Vue's slot iteration with explicit index binding.
