deferredItems.why: Low risk in practice (DOM structure is stable in slide templates), but good hygiene for future maintainability. Defer until next slide audit or when restructuring a specific slide.

deferredItems.item: Entrance reveal timing documentation: formalize the nextTick invariant and guarantee no async-mounted [data-reveal] elements exist
deferredItems.why: Architectural confirmation task, not a bug. Should be captured in a brief CLAUDE.md section on reveal guarantees. Prioritize if new slides introduce conditional reveals.

deferredItems.item: Slide authoring guide updates: document the glass-ui shadow composition pattern and child combinator rule
deferredItems.why: Living documentation. Capture the cohesion rules (tokens-only, child combinators, @container-only, no pasted colors/shadows) before the next slide deck is authored.

risks: No brittle combinator typos detected (the alleged Slide07 typo does not exist).
Reactivity is safe: [data-state] binding avoids querySelector fragility.
Design cohesion is strong across all 11 slides; no aesthetic drift from glass-ui.

Minor brittleness in two-tier descendant selectors (.presenter__people span, .snap .frozen) is acceptable given stable DOM structure in templates, but backporting child combinators is low-effort hygiene.
Animation entrance timing depends on nextTick, which is safe given the no-async-reveals invariant (should be documented).

findings.area: Slide06 mobile layout audit: layout hierarchy, icon spacing, negative space distribution
findings.summary: Slide06's mobile layout (two-pan balance scale + corner-case traps + caution) suffers from a fixed container query breakpoint strategy that creates visual squish and uneven negative space. The layout uses cqi-derived measurements that floor below optimal density on phones, oversized list gaps post-reflow, and a three-column balance-grid that stacks into single-column without responsive rhythm. The caution card and body gaps are generous but uncoordinated with the pan list spacing. A gestalt reflow should: (1) establish a coherent mobile rhythm via the deck's space-ladder (currently inconsistently applied); (2) densify pan list spacing to match visual hierarchy (8px list gap is excessive for 13px body text); (3) rebalance the fulcrum's visual weight as a stacked horizontal beam; (4) coordinate inter-element gaps via @container rules so the mobile rhythm reads as intentional, not accidental.

findings.title: Pan list gap spacing creates excessive vertical stretch on mobile
findings.evidence: Slide06.vue:294 `.pan ul { gap: var(--space-3); }` applies 10px gap to list items; line:296 `.pan li { font-size: clamp(13px, 2.7cqi, 17px); }` shows 13px base text. At 390px width, 2.7cqi ~= 10.3px (floor binds). Gap-to-text ratio 10:13 reads loose; paired with line-height 1.26, the list visually stretches vertically and competes with body layout for limited screen height.
findings.rootCause: The @container (width < 700px) block applies a uniform gap: var(--space-3) to all lists; space-3 (10px) was defined for inter-card rhythm (deck.css:214), not intra-list rhythm. The switch from cqi-derived gaps (desktop: calc(5*var(--cqx))) to fixed px was abrupt without recalibrating list-specific density.
findings.proposal: Reduce .pan ul gap from var(--space-3) to var(--space-2) on phones (8px, a √φ rung narrower). This preserves the leg-room above space-1 (6px, too tight for icon-bullet rhythm) while tightening vertical stretch. The gap-to-text ratio becomes 8:13 (cleaner proportional tension). Pair with: keep line-height:1.26 (reads generous within the tighter gap), keep 20px icon column (desktop is 16px*cqx; clamping to fixed prevents shrinkage), adjust SVG margin-top from 2px to 0 to remove pixel-level micro-adjustments that don't scale.

findings.title: Balance-grid column stacking loses visual separation at < 560px
findings.evidence: Slide06.vue:310-315: @container (width < 560px) { .balance-grid { grid-template-columns: 1fr; gap: var(--space-4); } } stacks the three-column layout (AI pan, fulcrum, People pan) into a single column with 13px (space-4) gap. At 360–390px (typical phones), the two pans are visually identical mirrors with only spacing between them; the fulcrum reorient to a 2px horizontal beam (line:314) spanning full width with no lateral break.
findings.rootCause: The portrait fulcrum reflow (line:313-314) hides the vertical post and shows the horizontal beam, but the beam's structural role as a 'separator + depth indicator' doesn't render with emphasis at small widths. The 13px gap between stacked pans is sized for body inter-card spacing, not for a semantic balance-scale motif where the fulcrum should read as a kinetic hinge. The beam loses visual hierarchy.
findings.proposal: Increase .balance-grid gap from var(--space-4) to var(--space-5) or var(--space-6) (17–22px) to give the horizontal beam breathing room and read as an intentional fulcrum moment, not just stack spacing. Enlarge .fulcrum height from calc(24*var(--cqx)) (≈19–21px on phone) to a fixed 32px so the beam pivot reads with presence. This preserves the motif's legibility: the beam becomes a visual landmark separating the two pans, not a hairline footnote. At 360px, the three-element stack (pan / beam / pan) then reads with clear hierarchy.

findings.title: Caution card padding inconsistently reflows against body and traps
findings.evidence: Slide06.vue:262-263 desktop: `.caution { padding: calc(13*var(--cqx)) calc(24*var(--cqx)); gap: calc(16*var(--cqx)); }` (≈52–61px padding, 64px gap at 1280). Line:305 mobile: `.caution { padding: var(--space-4) var(--space-5); gap: var(--space-4); margin-top: var(--space-6); }` (13px vertical, 17px horizontal, 22px above). Meanwhile .traps and .pan both get `padding: var(--space-3) var(--space-4)` (10x13px). The caution's 17px horizontal padding is 30% wider than the traps, creating visual misalignment.
findings.rootCause: The desktop caution was authored with generous padding (absolute cqx multiples) to weight it as a sentinel callout. The mobile reflow applied a mixed-scale approach: space-4 (13px) vertical reuses body rhythm, but space-5 (17px) horizontal doesn't align with the space-3/space-4 grid applied to .traps/.pan. The gap:space-4 (13px) is also narrower than the margin-top:space-6 (22px) above it, creating an inversion in the visual hierarchy.
findings.proposal: Unify caution card padding to match the body grid: `padding: var(--space-4) var(--space-4)` (13px square, matching .traps and .pan). Shift the visual weight via the gap: keep `gap: var(--space-5)` (17px) between icon and text to preserve the breathing room. Maintain `margin-top: var(--space-6)` (22px) to anchor the caution below the body. This aligns all card surfaces to the same left edge and establishes a consistent column measure, making the slide read as a unified composition rather than a scatter of ad-hoc frames.

findings.title: Fixed cqi-to-px conversion loses proportional scaling on narrow viewports
findings.evidence: Slide06.vue:295-299: @container (width < 700px) applies static px measures for icons (20px column, 16px svg) and text (clamp 13–17px, grid-template-columns: 20px 1fr, gap: var(--space-2)). At 360px width, 20px column is 5.5% of the measure; at 390px, it's 5.1%. Desktop uses calc(16*var(--cqx)) which scales proportionally as the canvas narrows. The floor clamp(13px, 2.7cqi, 17px) binds at ~384px (where 2.7cqi drops to 13px), so the whole measure collapses into a fixed-size layout just as the viewport becomes tightest.
findings.rootCause: The mobile reflow hardcodes pixel widths (20px icon column, 16px svg) to achieve consistent visual rhythm independent of cqi scaling. This is pragmatic for phones but introduces a breakpoint cliff: below 700px, the measure stops scaling with the container, and above 384px, the text also stops scaling. The icon column becomes proportionally oversized relative to available width, exacerbating the squish sensation.
findings.proposal: Replace hardcoded icon measures with cqi-derived clamps that maintain proportional rhythm: `.pan li { grid-template-columns: clamp(16px, 1.25cqi, 20px) 1fr; }` and `.pan li svg { width: clamp(14px, 1.09cqi, 16px); height: clamp(14px, 1.09cqi, 16px); }`. This restores proportional scaling: as the container narrows from 700px to 360px, the icon column scales from 20px → ~14px and the svg from 16px → ~11px, proportionally. The text clamp(13px, 2.7cqi, 17px) then reads as part of a coordinated scale, not an orphaned measure. At 360px, the measure doesn't feel as cramped because the icon column is no longer rigid.

findings.title: Trap layout padding and gap don't scale with mobile rhythm
findings.evidence: Slide06.vue:301-302: @container (width < 700px) applies `.traps { padding: var(--space-3) var(--space-4); }` and `.trap { padding-block: var(--space-2); }`. Each trap has 8px block padding (space-2) and a dashed border-top separator. The traps__cap margin-bottom uses the default cqi-derived calc(9*var(--cqx)) which still scales below 700px. On a 360px phone, the trap separator line reads visually prominent because the padding is tight (8px), but the intro cap is still cqi-scaled, creating an incoherent vertical rhythm.
findings.rootCause: The trap padding is sized for portrait spacing consistency (matching other cards), but the intro cap wasn't refactored in the @container block. Below 700px, the cap's margin-bottom (9cqx ≈ 7px at 360px) is tighter than the trap padding (8px block), creating a visual hiccup: the traps section heading pulls closer to its content than the spacing promises.
findings.proposal: Refactor the traps__cap margin-bottom in the @container (width < 700px) block: `@container (width < 700px) { .traps__cap { margin-bottom: var(--space-3); } }` to align with the traps__cap → trap flow (10px, matching .pan__rule margin). This ensures the heading-to-content flow reads as a single unit. If the current tight rhythm is intentional (bringing the trap labels closer to reader), reduce the trap padding-block to var(--space-1) (6px) for visual balance, pairing the heading's 10px drop with tighter internal padding.

findings.title: Excessive negative space above body on narrow portrait due to .slide padding + cqi margins
findings.evidence: Slide06.vue:283-290: @container (width < 700px) applies `.slide { padding: 6cqi 5cqi; }` (≈19–23px vertical at 360–700px range), .lede { margin-top: var(--space-1); } (6px), .body { margin-top: var(--space-4); } (13px). The header (line:7-10) includes eyebrow and chip, plus an implicit gap from the default .slide__header (deck.css:493) which uses margin-bottom:1.5rem (24px absolute). Below that: heading → lede → 13px gap → body. At 360px, the header + heading + lede occupy ~140px (35% of screen), leaving 220px for the balance grid + traps + caution, all with margins. The .case__head font-size clamp(27px, 6.4cqi, 50px) floors to 27px at ~340px, but the margin above (.slide padding) is still 6cqi ≈ 19px at 360px.
findings.rootCause: The slide padding (6cqi 5cqi) scales down to ~19px vertical on phones but is sized for landscape proportions. The header's 24px margin-bottom (absolute px from deck.css, not refactored in @container) creates a cumulative dead zone. The .lede margin-top (6px, space-1) is too tight, and .body margin-top (13px) doesn't compensate. The user reports 'excessive negative space' because these cqi-derived margins haven't been tightened proportionally to match the mobile rhythm (which uses fixed px like space-1..6).
findings.proposal: In @container (width < 700px), explicitly tighten the pre-body flow: `.case__head { margin-bottom: var(--space-3); }` (10px, not cqi-derived 5cqx). Update .lede { margin-top: var(--space-1); margin-bottom: var(--space-3); } to establish a clear drop from heading to lede (6px) then lede to body (10px), reading as a staircase not a plateau. Reduce .slide padding-top from 6cqi to 5cqi (mobile only) if the header needs tighter coupling, OR keep padding but enforce the margins as the true measure. The goal: header → heading → lede → body should read as a compact lead-in (≈50–60px total on a 360px phone), not 140px.

risks: Changing --space-2/3 values affects every slide's mobile reflow; audit other decks (Slide01-11) to ensure consistency before committing. Desktop portrait @media rules in other slides may assume the current space ladder.
Icon column clamps (F04) shift visual hierarchy; verify the balance-grid pans read as equal-weight at all widths. If the AI pan's icon grows relative to the People pan's icon, the scale motif breaks.
Fulcrum height increase (F02) from 24cqx to 32px is a threshold change; test at 360–560px to ensure it doesn't crowd the pan text or create unequal top/bottom margins in the balance-grid stack.
Caution padding unification (F03) reduces horizontal padding from 17px to 13px; watch for text wrapping changes if the caution paragraph content is long or uses narrow measure-sensitive hyphenation.

findings.area: Frontend-design audit: XRAY slide + portal (SL/src/decks/til-briefing/slides/Slide11.vue)
findings.summary: The XRAY portal (Slide11) currently exhibits three design issues: (1) the poster image has intrinsic aspect ratio 1.488:1 (2560×1720px) but mobile CSS locks it to 4:3 (1.333:1), creating letterboxing/white space; (2) the portal is embedded as a constrained portal within the slide grid, not full-viewport-height on mobile; (3) there is no "Open AI XRAY" button in the current codebase—the window container itself IS the launch mechanism (toggles from <a> on poster to <div> with live iframe on desktop). The design intent is sound (the poster and live frame coexist elegantly), but mobile needs full-height treatment to read as a feature, and the poster aspect ratio should match its intrinsic dimensions.

findings.title: Mobile portal constrained height—should fill viewport
findings.evidence: SL/src/decks/til-briefing/slides/Slide11.vue:213–228 mobile @container rule; SL/src/styles/deck.css:277–284 portrait slide scrolls; current mobile stack (.portal, .window) takes natural height within scrollable .slide, not full viewport
findings.rootCause: Mobile portal inherits the slide's block-flow layout (SL/src/styles/deck.css:277), so the portal stacks vertically but the window respects its flex-item constraints instead of claiming full available height. The window's `aspect-ratio: 4/3; align-self: stretch` works only if the slide context provides vertical flex budget; in portrait block flow, it collapses to content size.
findings.proposal: On mobile (@media max-aspect-ratio 1/1), force the portal to a full-screen overlay or modal treatment. Three options: (A) absolute positioning + fixed width portal that covers the viewport behind the dock clearance (simplest, idiomatic glass-ui pattern). (B) A new full-height wrapper that claims remaining viewport space via flex:1 + overflow auto. (C) Reflow the .rail and .window into separate full-height sections (rail scrolls to top, window takes remaining height). Option A (modal-like overlay triggered on-demand) aligns with the design intent (a 'live tool' exploration feel) and avoids scroll-within-scroll jank.

findings.title: Poster aspect ratio mismatch on mobile (1.489:1 image vs 4:3 CSS)
findings.evidence: SL/public/xray-poster.png is 2560×1720px (file command confirms), AR ≈ 1.4884:1; SL/src/decks/til-briefing/slides/Slide11.vue:224 applies `aspect-ratio: 4/3` (1.3333:1). The poster image (.poster, line 111) uses `object-fit: contain`, so the 4:3 locked container creates letterboxing (cream-colored borders above/below image).
findings.rootCause: Desktop CSS has no explicit aspect-ratio on .window; it flex:1-fills the grid column (relies on grid row-height). Mobile CSS hard-locks 4:3 to create a 'framed browser' appearance, but the actual poster source is wider (closer to 3:2 cinema). The mismatch was a deliberate design choice (frame smaller than source to read 'browser window'), but on mobile where height is precious, the wasted space (letterbox) hurts readability.
findings.proposal: Replace the hard-coded `aspect-ratio: 4/3` with `aspect-ratio: attr(data-aspect / 1)` bound to the image's computed AR, or more pragmatically, use `aspect-ratio: calc(2560 / 1720)` (match the poster source exactly via CSS custom property --xray-poster-ar: 1.489). This lets the image fill mobile width without letterboxing while preserving the browser-frame silhouette via the `object-fit: contain` + centered background. Validate that the LIVE iframe (when mounted on desktop) maintains readability at the same AR.

findings.title: No explicit 'Open AI XRAY' button—portal toggles via window container
findings.evidence: SL/src/decks/til-briefing/slides/Slide11.vue:87–113 shows no <Button> element. The <component :is="liveFrame ? 'div' : 'a'"> (line 87–88) IS the launch: when liveFrame is false (poster state), it renders as <a href=...> so tapping anywhere on the poster opens xray in a new tab; when liveFrame is true, it's a <div> with the live iframe. No separate button UI exists.
findings.rootCause: Design is intentionally minimalist: the 'window' frame itself (poster or iframe) is the affordance. This is elegant on desktop (the live iframe is obviously interactive) but ambiguous on mobile in poster state—users may not realize the entire poster image is tappable, and the visual hierarchy doesn't scream 'action' (the browser bar + status badge do, but no verb 'Open' or icon cue).
findings.proposal: No change needed to the portal logic. The current design (window-as-launch) is idiomatic and self-explanatory on desktop (LIVE iframe is clearly interactive). For mobile UX clarity, add a **subtle affordance cue** (not a button): either (1) a small tap-target overlay glyph (↗ icon, top-right of poster, only in poster state) that appears on hover/first-visit, or (2) enhance the status badge to include a verb 'TAP TO OPEN' when in poster state, replacing 'PREVIEW'. This keeps the design minimal while signaling intent. If a button is non-negotiable per requirements, add an small icon button (size: 'sm', variant: 'glass') below the poster with text 'Open in new tab' (visible only on mobile in poster state via `@media and (pointer: coarse)`), positioned absolutely bottom-right within the window frame.

risks: The poster image dimensions (2560×1720) are fixed; changing the CSS aspect-ratio will not reflow the source, so on narrow mobile the poster may appear blurry if upscaled. Mitigation: set max-width on the poster or ensure the source is large enough for 1x+ DPI. Validate visual quality at 390px–430px widths (typical mobile breakpoint).

Full-viewport portal on mobile (Proposal F1) requires careful management of the slide's scroll context—if the portal is fixed/absolute, it must account for the dock clearance (SL/src/styles/deck.css:266) to avoid overlap. The slide's scroll-padding-block-end already handles this for flow content; extend it or use inset:0 with a bottom margin.

The LIVE iframe (when xray is reachable on desktop) and the poster must stay aspect-ratio-synced if both are visible in the same session, otherwise viewport changes could trigger a visual pop. Verify this is not an issue in practice (active slide probe ensures only one is mounted at a time).

findings.area: constellation visibility audit: dark & light mode
findings.summary: The constellation lattice has asymmetric visibility problems in both modes. Light mode uses --constellation-alpha: 0.92 with edge strokes at 0.17×0.92 ≈ 0.16 effective (ghost-level), while dark mode at 1.0 reaches ≈0.17 on cream foreground. The accent red is anchored to --ncsu-red (#cc0000) in both—graphical-strength on dark canvas, but underpowered on cream. The proposal: per-mode alphas (dark: 1.0 stays; light: 0.95), per-mode accent lifting (light: --ncsu-red-bright for +50% chroma), and optional glow on the anomaly ring for enhanced presence without garish reads.

findings.title: Light mode: constellation edges ghost-level despite 0.92 alpha
findings.evidence: constellation.ts:250-251 `ctx.globalAlpha = (red ? 0.26 * t + 0.07 : 0.17 * t) * this.alpha`; deck.css:190 `--constellation-alpha: 0.92`; effective alpha on neutral lattice = 0.17 × 0.92 ≈ 0.156 on cream (hsl 48 12% 98% / L98) over cream background (L98) reads as no lattice
findings.rootCause: Light mode reserve: the cream-ground text must clear the field, so constellation alpha is intentionally suppressed to stay below type readability. At 0.92, the node/edge strokes reach only WCAG AAA barely-perceptible threshold. The audit lifted from 0.72→0.92 in F.W4/V06, but the curve still doesn't surface the geometry clearly enough on light canvas.
findings.proposal: Lift light-mode alpha to 0.95 (3% increment from 0.92), keeping the accent under control. At 0.95, neutral lines reach ≈0.16 effective (perceptual floor holding). Pair with a per-mode accent strategy: light mode reads --ncsu-red-bright (#e6322a) for the anomaly + edge connections, so the red amplifies contrast against cream without tuning the node white-alpha separately. Revert anomaly edges to accentColor (red) in light mode only; neutral edges stay neutral.

findings.title: Dark mode: accent red is underweight on ink canvas despite full alpha
findings.evidence: constellation.ts:250 edge stroke reads `this.accentColor` (--constellation-accent, aliased to --ncsu-red #cc0000); deck.css:196 `--constellation-accent: var(--ncsu-red)` pinned to #cc0000; dark foreground is hsl(48 10% 90%) on ink-950 (hsl(20 16% 7%)). At full alpha (1.0) the red pulse + tether reach ≈0.28 effective but the hue sits at chroma 72% (SRGB saturation), reading subdued against the warm-cream type contrast.
findings.rootCause: Dark mode has full alpha headroom (1.0 vs light's 0.92), but the accent color is locked to a graphical-strength red (#cc0000) that reads as MUTED against the lighter cream-on-ink foreground (L90). The anomaly's pulse + pulsing ring (alpha: 0.5, 0.7 respectively) are load-bearing visual cues, but the ambient hue doesn't pop enough for a glance to land on the anomaly as the focal point.
findings.proposal: Upgrade dark mode accent to a warmer, brighter red: shift --constellation-accent to --ncsu-red-bright (#e6332a) in dark mode only (via deck.css `.dark` override). This lifts the hue to 70% chroma with +7% luminance, reads as a warm accent against the cream type, and creates visual hierarchy without breaking the neutral lattice. The anomaly pulse rings already use the accent at variable opacity; brighten the base color, not the alphas. Keep light mode on --ncsu-red (the original), shifting only the dark arm.

findings.title: Anomaly pulsing ring opacity insufficient in both modes
findings.evidence: constellation.ts:284-289 anomaly pulse ring: `ctx.globalAlpha = (1 - phase) * 0.5` at peak phase=0 → alpha=0.5; inner fixed ring at `ctx.globalAlpha = 0.7`. Combined with accent color + 1.1px stroke, the rings read as soft glows, not focal marks. In light mode (0.92 alpha multiply) the rings reach ≈0.46 and ≈0.64 effective; in dark mode at 1.0 they stay at 0.5/0.7.
findings.rootCause: The anomaly is pinned in dead space (data-anomaly='0.72,0.36' for Slide01, '0.46,0.30' for Slide10) to avoid type occlusion, but the pulsing ring is the only visual anchor tethering the pinned node to the field. At 0.5 peak alpha the glow reads as ambient, not anomalous. The label tether (0.6 alpha dashed line, constellation.ts:316) reads louder than the ring.
findings.proposal: Lift anomaly pulse ring opacity: peak phase alpha from 0.5→0.65 (the inner ring stays 0.7), so the breathing glow reads as a deliberate pulse even when subdued by the per-mode alpha multiplier. At 0.65 peak the light-mode rings reach ≈0.60 effective (legible glow), dark mode at ≈0.65 (stronger presence). No glyph redesign; the curve stays quadratic (1 - phase), just the ceiling lifts. Optional: add a faint secondary glow (blur via CSS filter on the canvas, or a soft halo at 0.2 alpha 2× the ring radius) for dark mode anomaly only, reading as a soft catch-light under dark surfaces.

findings.title: No per-mode accent strategy: --constellation-accent frozen at --ncsu-red
findings.evidence: constellation.ts:103 `this.accentColor = readVar(c, '--constellation-accent', '#cc0000')` reads the CSS variable once at palette(). deck.css:196 `--constellation-accent: var(--ncsu-red)` never branches on `.dark`. The anomaly ring, edges touching the anomaly, and the label tether all consume this single color in both modes.
findings.rootCause: The design system (glass-ui's red tokens, deck.css's --ncsu-red-*) already supplies a full red register: --ncsu-red (#cc0000 graphical, 3:1 bar), --ncsu-red-bright (#e6322a for small/normal text, AA legible on ink). The constellation abstains from this register—it locks to one red, missing the opportunity for per-mode contrast tuning. The MutationObserver at constellation.ts:432-439 does re-call palette() when color-scheme flips, so the system is BUILT to support dark-aware tokens.
findings.proposal: Express --constellation-accent as a light-dark() pair in deck.css. Light arm: var(--ncsu-red) (#cc0000, graphical strength on cream). Dark arm: var(--ncsu-red-bright) (#e6322a, text-legible on ink, warmer hue, higher chroma). Constellation.ts readVar() consumes the resolved value unchanged—no code change required, pure CSS token lift. The MutationObserver will re-sample the flipped accent on theme toggle, painting the anomaly in the new hue instantly.

findings.title: Light mode text contrast headroom underutilized for accent visibility
findings.evidence: deck.css:184-189 comment: `the constellation field is decorative and must YIELD to slide type—this alpha multiplier dims the lattice in light mode (where cream-ground text sits over it)...Lifted 0.72→0.92 (F.W4/V06): at 0.72 the LIGHT line strokes reached only 0.17×0.72≈0.12 effective (ghost-level—the triangulation was absent); 0.92 brings them to ≈0.16 so the lattice reads as a deliberate motif while staying below the type.` The comment acknowledges the tension: higher alpha → motif reads, but type legibility is the hard floor.
findings.rootCause: The constellation plays a supporting role on Slide01/Slide10 (the only slides that carry it). The canvas is masked (Slide01.vue:69-70 mask-image linear-gradient 105deg fading off) so the constellation never occludes the type. The masking + dedicated dead-space anchors (data-anomaly attributes) already reserve the right side for the motif. The alpha is conservative, assuming global occlusion, but the masking + layout already bought visibility headroom.
findings.proposal: Bump light-mode alpha from 0.92→0.95 (a 3% lift), trusting the mask + layout to clear type. The effective line alpha reaches ≈0.1605 (just 1 basis-point above current), staying in the 'legible motif' band but reading with gentler weight. Pair this micro-increment with the per-mode accent lift (P1 proposal G2) so the red anomaly pops against the lattice without the lattice becoming garish. The micro-increment is SAFE—it reads as the same deliberate motif, just 1 notch clearer.

risks: Accent color brightness: --ncsu-red-bright (#e6322a) on ink canvas reaches L90 cream foreground at ≈6.5:1 contrast (WCAG AAA). The hue shift (6°→359° in HSL red-saturation) is subtle but real. Verify the dark-mode anomaly reads as 'warm accent', not 'lighter red' in context. Light mode --ncsu-red (#cc0000) on cream (L98) reaches ≈5.23:1 (AA floor); accent edges in light mode are graphical-strength, not body text, so the bar is 3:1 (WCAG G18)—both modes clear.

Per-mode alpha asymmetry: light 0.95 / dark 1.0 creates a ~5% brightness delta on the lattice field alone. Given that dark mode's cream type is 8-9 L° brighter than light mode's foreground (L90 vs L10), this delta is INTENTIONAL—the headroom is real and unequal. Docstring the token pair (constellation-alpha: light vs dark) so future audits understand the asymmetry is by design.

Anomaly ring opacity lift (0.5→0.65 peak) interacts with the canvas multiply path: each frame re-resolves `phase` from the RAF timestamp, so the ring breathes continuously. At 0.65 peak the inner ring (fixed 0.7) becomes less-dominant visually; verify the reading in context (the inner ring should stay as the 'found' confirmation mark, outer as the 'pulsing' beat). If the breathing feels muddied, cap the lift at 0.60 instead.

Optional glow halo on dark-mode anomaly: if added via CSS filter drop-shadow on the canvas element, it applies globally to the entire constellation (all strokes + fills), not just the anomaly—over-rendering. If added in-canvas, it requires a 6th render pass (drawGlow() before drawAnomaly()). Either approach is load-bearing. Recommend documenting the trade-off: glow amplifies focal presence but costs either global canvas blur or render overhead. Defer glow unless field testing shows the 0.65 peak alpha + bright accent insufficient.

findings.area: til-briefing slides (Slide01-Slide11): frontend-design audit of SVG/canvas data-viz components for mobile aspect-ratio integrity, visual hierarchy, occlusion, and responsive reflow.
findings.summary: The til-briefing slide deck contains 11 slides with complex data-visualization components (SVG canvases, progress gauges, flow diagrams, waveforms, and charts). Mobile responsiveness is broadly well-designed via @container queries (700px breakpoint) and cqi-based typography, but three high-priority aspect-ratio and responsive-design issues emerged: (1) Slide09's waveform (wave-wrap) uses flex auto-height on desktop, causing aspect-ratio collapse on mobile portrait below the specified 3/1 ratio; (2) Slide07's progress gauge lacks portrait aspect-ratio constraint, allowing the arc SVG to distort; (3) Slide08's feedback arc uses viewBox="1136 296" with preserveAspectRatio="none", causing path coordinate shearing on non-16:9 mobile ratios. All detected issues have idiomatic, KISS fixes grounded in Tailwind-first responsive design principles.

findings.title: Wave-wrap aspect-ratio collapse on mobile portrait
findings.evidence: /Users/mkbabb/Programming/slides/src/decks/til-briefing/slides/Slide09.vue:299 — `.wave-wrap { aspect-ratio: 3 / 1; }` defined ONLY inside @container (width < 700px) block. On desktop, wave-wrap is a flex child with `flex: 1 1 auto; min-height: 0` (line 225), so on portrait breakpoint it transitions from flex-expanding to a constrained 3:1, BUT the parent (.present) has no explicit height, causing the svg to squish vertically as it reflows.
findings.rootCause: wave-wrap's aspect-ratio rule is conditional-only (portrait block); desktop has no aspect-ratio constraint. When the layout reflows from desktop's two-column scope → portrait's one-column, the SVG aspect ratio is never enforced on transition. The path d='M0 39 L24 35...' (line 50) with viewBox='0 0 600 72' assumes a ~8.3:1 ratio; when the container height shrinks without aspect-ratio pinning, the anomaly spike at x=412 shears sideways instead of reading as a vertical event.
findings.proposal: Add `aspect-ratio: auto 8.33 / 1;` to desktop `.wave-wrap { position: relative; flex: 1 1 auto; min-height: 0; margin-top: calc(8*var(--cqx)); aspect-ratio: auto 8.33 / 1; }` so the 8.3:1 viewBox ratio is honored on both desktop and portrait. The 3/1 portrait override (line 299) then becomes the narrowing constraint, not a conflicting rule. Rationale: the SVG's coordinate space (600 wide, 72 tall) is intrinsically 8.33:1; preserveAspectRatio='none' distorts only when the container violates that ratio.

findings.title: Progress gauge SVG lacks portrait aspect-ratio enforcement
findings.evidence: /Users/mkbabb/Programming/slides/src/decks/til-briefing/slides/Slide07.vue:228 — `.gauge__svg { width: 100%; max-width: calc(292*var(--cqx)); height: auto; overflow: visible; }` has NO aspect-ratio rule. The SVG viewBox='0 0 280 290' is ~0.96:1 (nearly square), but the SVG is absolutely centered in .gauge (line 225, `display: grid; place-items: center`). On portrait, the gauge container shrinks to fit the narrow column, and `height: auto` allows the arc to compress vertically, distorting the 270° sweep geometry (center point at 140,140 assumes square aspect).
findings.rootCause: SVG viewBox defines geometry (280×290 = 0.96:1 aspect), but CSS applies no constraint. On desktop, the grid container is wide enough that `max-width: calc(292*var(--cqx))` caps the expansion; on portrait, there is no min/max height applied, so the flex parent (.hero, line 156) can shrink the gauge vertically. The arc track path (line 89, center 140,140, radius 110) and milestone circles (97, 103) assume the viewBox aspect is preserved; any vertical squish breaks the arc alignment.
findings.proposal: Add explicit aspect-ratio to .gauge__svg: `.gauge__svg { width: 100%; max-width: calc(292*var(--cqx)); aspect-ratio: 280 / 290; height: auto; overflow: visible; }` OR adopt a mobile-safe SVG aspect pin via inline style on the SVG (line 79): `viewBox='0 0 280 290' preserveAspectRatio='xMidYMid meet'` (already declared in the template, so CSS rule alone suffices). The aspect-ratio rule ensures the intrinsic SVG geometry is honored at all viewport widths.

findings.title: Feedback loop arc SVG shears on non-16:9 mobile viewports
findings.evidence: /Users/mkbabb/Programming/slides/src/decks/til-briefing/slides/Slide08.vue:22 — `.feedback { viewBox='0 0 1136 296' preserveAspectRatio='none' }` fills the entire .loop container (absolute inset:0, line 346). The viewBox is 1136×296 ≈ 3.84:1 (landscape/16:9-ish ratio). On portrait mobile (e.g., iPhone 390×844), the viewBox aspect (3.84:1) is forced to stretch/compress to match the portrait aspect (~0.46:1), causing the curved return arc path (line 26, M 1066 252 C ... L 102 290) to shear horizontally. The cubic-Bézier curve control points are authored for the landscape viewBox; when stretching to portrait, the arc flattens and the HANDOFF label text (line 28) skews.
findings.rootCause: preserveAspectRatio='none' on a landscape-biased viewBox (3.84:1) applied to a portrait container forces extreme non-uniform scaling. The path coordinates (x: 1066→54, y: 252→290) and the cubic handles assume the original 1136×296 aspect; the text anchor (x='568', y='278') is centered for landscape but appears off-center when the viewBox is squished to portrait. The @container portrait block (line 390) already hides the feedback element (display: none), so the occlusion is handled—but if the hide were ever removed, the shear would be severe.
findings.proposal: The .feedback is already correctly hidden on portrait via `display: none` in @container (width < 700px) block (line 393). NO CHANGE NEEDED on the SVG itself. However, to make the SVG responsive-safe for future use or edge-case viewports: replace `preserveAspectRatio='none'` with `preserveAspectRatio='xMidYMid slice'` or `'xMidYMid meet'`, and add a .loop container constraint: `.loop { aspect-ratio: auto 1136 / 296; }` so the feedback SVG viewBox aspect is always honored. Current code is correct (feedback is hidden on mobile), but this fix hardens against future refactor.

findings.title: Ledger and delta SVGs use preserveAspectRatio='none' on landscape-only backgrounds
findings.evidence: /Users/mkbabb/Programming/slides/src/decks/til-briefing/slides/Slide04.vue:8 — `.ledger { viewBox='0 0 1280 720' preserveAspectRatio='none' }` positioned absolutely (inset: 0, line 100) as a faint watermark. On portrait, the viewBox 1280×720 (16:9) is stretched to portrait aspect, shearing the vertical ledger lines (x-coords stay pinned; y-coords stretch 2.6×). However, the .ledger has `opacity: 0.5` and a mask gradient (line 102-103), so visual occlusion is acceptable. The delta__svg (line 37) uses `preserveAspectRatio='xMidYMid meet'`, which is correct and DOES NOT distort.
findings.rootCause: preserveAspectRatio='none' on a landscape viewBox (1280×720) applied to a portrait slide container forces the SVG to fill the inset:0 box without respecting aspect, shearing ledger line angles. The lines are horizontal (y1/y2 coordinates constant; x1/x2 span 1280), so stretching the y-axis doesn't affect them visually—they remain horizontal. BUT the grid pattern and spacing FEEL off if the user rotates or views on an ultra-wide desktop where the y-stretch is extreme. The mask gradient (lines 102-103) intelligently fades the ledger, so even if sheared, it's cosmetic background noise.
findings.proposal: Change line 8 to preserve landscape aspect: `<svg class='ledger' viewBox='0 0 1280 720' preserveAspectRatio='xMidYMid slice' aria-hidden='true'>` and add a .slide container aspect-ratio constraint OR accept the current behavior (watermark is faint and masked, so distortion is imperceptible). No user-facing fix required; the ledger is a purely decorative atmosphere. Recommendation: DEFER unless the art direction changes.

findings.title: Tape watermark SVG distorts on portrait; receipt and perforated-edge SVGs are responsive-safe
findings.evidence: /Users/mkbabb/Programming/slides/src/decks/til-briefing/slides/Slide05.vue:8 — `.tape { viewBox='0 0 1280 720' preserveAspectRatio='none' }` (same as S04 ledger). The perf SVGs (lines 38, 52) use `preserveAspectRatio='none'` but are CONSTRAINED: `.perf { width: 100%; height: calc(7*var(--cqx)); }` (line 171) with explicit height, so aspect ratio is pinned by the height constraint regardless of viewBox—the width stretches but the path stays within the fixed 7cqi height. The receipt itself is rotated and scaled via transform (line 156), so its SVG aspect is not a responsive concern.
findings.rootCause: The .tape watermark (line 116) is absolutely positioned (inset: 0) like the ledger, so it stretches to fill the slide. The viewBox 1280×720 distorts to portrait. However, the mask gradient (lines 119-120) fades it off-screen, so visual impact is minimal. The perf SVGs, by contrast, have explicit height constraints that lock the aspect ratio despite `preserveAspectRatio='none'`—they are responsive-safe by design.
findings.proposal: Same as S04: change to `preserveAspectRatio='xMidYMid slice'` for consistency and defensive design, or DEFER because the visual impact is minimal (masked, faint background). The perf SVGs are ALREADY CORRECT and require no change.

findings.title: Balance-grid fulcrum SVGs reflow correctly on portrait; no aspect-ratio fix needed
findings.evidence: /Users/mkbabb/Programming/slides/src/decks/til-briefing/slides/Slide06.vue:49 (fulcrum__beam) and 53 (fulcrum__hbeam) both use `preserveAspectRatio='none'` with explicit width/height props (width='8' height='100' and width='100' height='8'). The @container portrait block (line 310-315) swaps visibility: `.fulcrum__beam { display: none; }` and `.fulcrum__hbeam { display: block; }` on narrow screens. The layout reflow is INTENTIONAL and CORRECT—the vertical post becomes a horizontal beam, and no aspect-ratio distortion occurs because the SVG content is simple (single lines) that adapt to their container dimensions.
findings.rootCause: N/A—no issue. The fulcrum SVGs are responsive-by-design: the viewBox='0 0 8 100' and viewBox='0 0 100 8' are swapped visually via CSS display/hide, not CSS scaling. The line stroke stays 1-2px regardless of the viewBox scaling.
findings.proposal: NO CHANGE. This is exemplar responsive SVG design: intentional reflow via display rules, not aspect-ratio hacks. Document as a reference pattern for future complex slides.

findings.title: Cover constellation canvas has portrait-specific mask; no aspect-ratio issue
findings.evidence: /Users/mkbabb/Programming/slides/src/decks/til-briefing/slides/Slide01.vue:7 — `<canvas class='scatter' ... />` (line 72) is a full-inset canvas with a CSS mask gradient. The @container portrait block (lines 186-207) changes the mask gradient angle (line 198, `mask-image: linear-gradient(195deg, ...)` from 105deg) to adapt the constellation motif's drift direction. No aspect-ratio issue; the canvas fills the slide and the mask adapts the animation.
findings.rootCause: N/A—no issue. The canvas uses JavaScript to render points and is aware of its own dimensions at runtime; CSS aspect-ratio constraints don't apply to canvas elements (they have implicit 2D context). The mask gradient reflow is intentional and correct.
findings.proposal: NO CHANGE. Document as exemplar use of mask-gradient reflow for atmosphere layers.

findings.title: Snapshot past SVG (.snap) and waveform present SVG both responsive-safe; wave-wrap parent is the failure point
findings.evidence: /Users/mkbabb/Programming/slides/src/decks/til-briefing/slides/Slide09.vue:26 (.snap) and 44 (.wave, lines 44, 61) both use `preserveAspectRatio='none'` but are CONSTRAINED by their parent containers. The .snap is `width: 100%; height: 28` (line 194, implicit height ~28px), which locks aspect ratio. The .wave SVGs are positioned absolutely inside .wave-wrap (line 227-228), which is the parent container with flex/aspect-ratio applied. The SVG itself is responsive-safe; the issue is .wave-wrap's aspect-ratio rule is only on portrait (line 299), leaving the desktop wave-wrap unsized on tall slides.
findings.rootCause: See S09-001. The wave-wrap lacks an aspect-ratio rule on desktop, so the SVG can expand/contract freely, collapsing on reflow when entering portrait. The SVG preserveAspectRatio='none' is INTENTIONAL (as noted in the comment line 42: 'viewBox aspect (~8.3:1) now matches the rendered box'), but the parent container must enforce that 8.3:1 ratio at all breakpoints.
findings.proposal: Implement S09-001 fix: add `aspect-ratio: auto 8.33 / 1;` to desktop .wave-wrap rule (line 225), and the portrait override (line 299) becomes a narrowing constraint, not a conflicting rule. This ensures the SVG's intrinsic geometry is honored on both desktop and mobile.

findings.title: Anomaly landscape tile SVGs are responsive-safe; glyph sizing reflows correctly
findings.evidence: /Users/mkbabb/Programming/slides/src/decks/til-briefing/slides/Slide03.vue — Six inline SVG glyphs (width='28' height='28' viewBox='0 0 28 28') inside .glyph containers (line 204-210). The @container portrait block (line 243-248) adjusts .glyph to use `clamp(32px, 9cqi, 46px)` instead of calc-based sizing. Each glyph's SVG has no preserveAspectRatio attribute (defaults to xMidYMid meet), so aspect ratio is preserved. Responsive reflow works correctly.
findings.rootCause: N/A—no issue. The glyphs are small inlined SVGs with fixed 1:1 aspect (viewBox='0 0 28 28'), and the container constrains them symmetrically. No distortion.
findings.proposal: NO CHANGE. Document the glyph pattern as exemplar responsive SVG sizing.

risks: S09's wave-wrap aspect-ratio fix must NOT introduce a hard height constraint that causes overflow on short tablets or landscape phones; use `aspect-ratio: auto 8.33 / 1;` with `flex: 1 1 auto; min-height: 0;` to allow flex shrinking.

S07's gauge aspect-ratio rule must respect the .gauge's grid centering; adding aspect-ratio to .gauge__svg does NOT affect the parent, so the SVG may overflow its grid cell on ultra-narrow phones (<360px). Test at 320px viewport.

S08's feedback arc is already hidden on portrait (@container display:none), so no runtime shear occurs; do NOT remove the hide rule. If the arc is ever made visible on mobile, the shear fix becomes critical.

preserveAspectRatio='none' on landscape viewBox (S04, S05 ledger/tape) is intentional for full-bleed watermarks, but future use of this pattern on content SVGs (not backgrounds) will cause user-visible distortion. Document the watermark-only constraint in code comments.
The @container (width < 700px) breakpoint applies to slide container width (cqi-based), not viewport width; test on actual slide player, not raw viewport simulators, to verify mobile rendering.

deferredItems.item: S04 ledger watermark SVG preserveAspectRatio='none' → 'xMidYMid slice'
deferredItems.why: The ledger is a faint, fully-masked atmospheric background layer (opacity: 0.5, mask-image gradient). The viewBox distortion (1280×720 stretched to portrait) does not affect user-visible content, and the mask gradient fades it away. Distortion is imperceptible. Fold into a future design-refinement pass.

deferredItems.item: S05 tape watermark SVG preserveAspectRatio='none' → 'xMidYMid slice'
deferredItems.why: Same rationale as S04: the tape is a faint, masked watermark. Visual impact is minimal. The perf SVGs (perforated edges on the receipt) are already responsive-safe by explicit height constraints and require NO CHANGE. Fold into a future design-refinement pass when atmosphere tightening is warranted.

findings.area: Frontend-design audit: access-key modal (DeckGate.vue) + locked-deck homepage cards (HomeView.vue)
findings.summary: The access-key unlock modal and locked-deck homepage affordances are styled coherently but lack full glass-ui design system integration. DeckGate.vue uses glass-ui Dialog with a stylized center-mounted form, while HomeView.vue's locked cards employ decorative scrim overlays with backdrop-filter blur. A cohesive redesign should: (1) enhance the modal's visual weight via the glass-floating surface with refined red identity (--ncsu-red, --red-wash, --red-text tokens already aligned); (2) introduce a bespoke lock-screen visual metaphor (concentric circles, subtle gradient depth, hand-crafted lock icon placement); and (3) unify the homepage card blur states to match the modal's glass aesthetic, ensuring a paired narrative between "waiting to unlock" (at rest on home) and "unlocking now" (modal interaction).

findings.title: DeckGate modal lacks visual lock-screen identity
findings.evidence: DeckGate.vue:38-69 — Dialog with DialogContent class="deck-gate" houses a .deck-gate__lock circle glyph (LockKeyhole SVG, 28px, styled with --red-wash + --red-tint-15), a Fraunces title, prose description, password Input, and Button with variant="primary-audacious". The modal currently reads as a generic confirmation dialog, not a befitting lock-screen interface. deck.css §8 (lines 734-782) styles the gate: a centered text-align, the lock disc (grid place-items-center, 3.25rem size, red tint wash), and a shake animation on failed submission.
findings.rootCause: The current design treats the modal as generic form chrome rather than leveraging the deck's warm-cream/red glassmorphism identity and cartoon-shadow depth language. No lock-screen visual narrative (layering, visual weight progression, branded moment).
findings.proposal: Redesign DeckGate as a cohesive lock-screen experience: (1) Enhance the .deck-gate__lock glyph—render concentric circles (outer subtle glass disc, inner red-washed chamber with keyhole) with 1px red hairline borders and inner box-shadow depth to suggest 'locked vault'. (2) Upgrade the DialogContent to layer a subtle red radial gradient background beneath the glass-floating tier (NOT opaque—preserve the glass aesthetic, but add visual weight via --glass-bg-floating + a contained radial-red wash at the DialogContent root). (3) Tighten .deck-gate__head margin and compose the lock glyph as a focal point subordinate to the Fraunces title (already correct at --d margin). (4) Style the Input field with a red-wash border on focus (alias --red-tint-15 → border-color, inherit focus ring from glass-ui's existing [aria-invalid] pattern at line 770-772). (5) Keep the primary-audacious Button (hero accent), but ensure it reads at 44px touch-target min (WCAG 2.5.8). Use the existing .deck-gate form layout (gap 0.75rem, margin-top 0.25rem) but refine spacing via the φ ladder. (6) Export the lock glyph concentric-circle SVG with variable --lock-scale and --lock-color for reuse on the homepage.

findings.title: Locked deck cards lack cohesive blur surface treatment paired with modal
findings.evidence: HomeView.vue:20-44 — Deck gallery renders a .home__grid (grid auto-fill minmax 320px) of RouterLink cards. Each .deck-card (flex column, gap 0.6rem, padding 1.6rem 1.7rem) has a child .deck-card__scrim (lines 35-41) for locked decks: position absolute inset:0, border-radius inherit, flex center, pointer-events:none, opacity:0 transitioning on hover/focus. The scrim uses backdrop-filter blur(2.5px) with -webkit- prefix and a color-mix bg (var(--background) 32%, transparent). The scrim never reads as cohesive with the modal's red identity—it's a neutral frosted blur, not a 'locked' visual statement.
findings.rootCause: The scrim treatment is decorative frosting (neutral blur + darkened wash) rather than a cohesive glass-ui themed surface that echoes the lock-screen modal's warm-cream/red identity. The homepage lacks a visual throughline: the gated cards are merely blurred on hover, not branded as 'locked awaiting key'.
findings.proposal: Redesign .deck-card__scrim to be a coherent glass surface that mirrors the modal's lock experience: (1) Replace neutral color-mix(var(--background) 32%, transparent) with a red-tinted wash: color-mix(in srgb, var(--ncsu-red) 18%, transparent) so the blur implies 'gated by red' without obscuring the card. (2) Render the lock icon as a foreground element with size 28px (matching modal), styled with --red-text foreground. (3) Preserve backdrop-filter blur(2.5px) — it's already at rest and harmonizes with the glass ladder. (4) Layer a subtle inner box-shadow on the scrim to suggest depth: inset 0 0 12px color-mix(in srgb, var(--ncsu-red) 8%, transparent). (5) Transition the scrim opacity on :hover/:focus-visible with the existing 0.24s var(--ease-standard), so the locked-state reveal is snappy. (6) Add a companion .deck-card__tag--lock styling refinement: increase letter-spacing to match deck.css .eyebrow (var(--track-caps) = 0.16em) so the 'access key' chip reads as official deck chrome, not a generic badge.

findings.title: Lock experience should cite glass-ui's @theme aliases for semantic surfaces
findings.evidence: deck.css §1 (lines 22-136) defines --ncsu-red (hero), --ncsu-red-deep, --ncsu-red-bright, --ncsu-red-ink, --red-wash (9% tint), --red-tint-15 (15% tint), --red-tint-30, --red-text. glass-ui's theme.css lines 123-125 map --color-surface-tint-quiet (--surface-tint-6 ≈ 6%), --color-surface-tint-floating (--surface-tint-12 ≈ 12%), --color-surface-tint-modal (--surface-tint-18 ≈ 18%). The modal could leverage these Tailwind-bridged aliases instead of hand-rolling color-mix().
findings.rootCause: The current DeckGate.vue and HomeView.vue styles use direct color-mix() expressions (e.g., deck.css line 756 uses --red-wash, which is color-mix(in srgb, var(--ncsu-red) 9%, transparent)). While correct, this decouples the lock experience from glass-ui's semantic surface tier system, making future token adjustments brittle.
findings.proposal: Cite Tailwind @theme aliases in the glass-ui Tailwind config or declare scoped --lock-surface-* tokens at :root in deck.css (§1, after --red-text). Example: --lock-surface-wash: var(--red-wash) [already exists]; --lock-surface-tint: color-mix(in srgb, var(--ncsu-red) 15%, transparent). Then compose DeckGate via `class="bg-surface-tint-modal"` and .deck-card__scrim via inline style `background: var(--lock-surface-tint)`. This lifts the lock experience into the glass-ui tier vocabulary, ensuring coherence if the red register or surface opacity ever shifts. (Note: This is an optional refactoring—current direct color-mix() is idiomatic for the deck's bespoke red identity.)

findings.title: Lock icon on homepage card scrim must be aria-hidden and never trap interaction
findings.evidence: HomeView.vue:35-41 — The .deck-card__scrim already has aria-hidden="true" and pointer-events: none in CSS, preventing interaction trapping. The LockKeyhole SVG (line 40, size 26, stroke-width 1.75) is properly subordinate. This is correct.
findings.rootCause: No issue—the current implementation is accessible. Confirming for completeness.
findings.proposal: Maintain the existing accessibility model: the scrim is decorative (aria-hidden), never dismissible, and pointer-events:none ensures clicks pass through to the underlying RouterLink. The lock glyph is a visual affordance, not interactive. No change required.

findings.title: Lock glyph and scrim must degrade gracefully in ?export / ?print mode
findings.evidence: deck.css §9 (lines 815-855) handles body.export-mode and body.print-mode. The .slide::after paper-grain (line 301-310) persists via mix-blend-mode. The homepage (not a slide) and DeckGate modal (teleported DialogPortal, outside the slide tree) have no explicit export-mode rules. In ?export, the modal should either hide entirely (non-dismissable gate can never resolve) or remain visible with the full glass surfaces (context-dependent).
findings.rootCause: DeckGate is a non-dismissable blocker; in ?export mode, the modal would orphan the export—the gate never unlocks, so no deck content exports. The homepage gallery (?export=home or similar) might export the locked-card scrims as frosted boxes, which is fine.
findings.proposal: Add a rule in deck.css §9 (after line 823): `body.export-mode .deck-gate { display: none; }` to hide the gate in export mode (the gate cannot resolve without JavaScript interaction, and the deck chunk won't load without unlock—the export would be blank anyway). For the homepage gallery, .deck-card__scrim is already opacity:0 at rest, so export-mode renders the cards without the scrim overlay (correct—export shows the unlock state as 'blurred card', not the interactive hover state). No additional styling needed.

findings.title: Unified visual narrative: 'locked awaiting key' from home to modal
findings.evidence: Currently: HomeView locked cards show a neutral frosted scrim + lock icon on hover. DeckGate modal shows a red-washed form with a lock glyph. The two experiences are visually disjoint—hovering a locked card doesn't 'promise' the modal you're about to see. The lock icon on the card (26px) is slightly smaller than the modal's (28px), and the scrim's neutral wash doesn't echo the modal's red identity.
findings.rootCause: Independent design iterations without a cohesive system narrative. Each component solves 'how do we show locked?' locally without considering the user's journey from 'locked card on home' → 'click → unlock modal'.
findings.proposal: Design a unified lock experience arc: (1) At rest on the homepage, a locked card reads as 'this content is gated' via the lock-chip tag (already styled .deck-card__tag--lock with --red-text + --red-wash). (2) On hover, the .deck-card__scrim fades in with a red-tinted glass surface (matching the modal's backdrop) + a 28px lock glyph (matching the modal's exact icon), creating a visual promise: 'interact here to unlock with a key'. (3) Clicking navigates to the deck page, which renders the non-dismissable modal—the scrim's red wash + lock icon are now full-screen, with the modal's Fraunces title + input form. The narrative is: locked (card) → click → locked (modal, more insistent) → enter key → unlocked. This arc requires: (a) .deck-card__scrim lock icon size: 28px (currently 26px, trivial tweak). (b) .deck-card__scrim background: red-tinted wash matching .deck-gate__lock's --red-wash tone. (c) .deck-gate__lock rendered as an SVG-based concentric lock symbol (upgrade from plain LockKeyhole) to reinforce the 'vault' metaphor.

risks: Changing --red-wash opacity or the red color token will require synchronized updates to both DeckGate and HomeView scrim styling—document the token as 'lock experience primary tint' to signal its use.
The concentric-lock SVG for the modal glyph is a new asset; ensure it loads without network overhead and respects the --cqx scale on the deck (or export mode will render at wrong size).
The scrim's red tint may reduce card readability if the background image or content is already red-heavy; test with red-dominant deck titles on the homepage gallery.
Adding backdrop-filter blur to the homepage scrim (already present) may impact performance on older devices; the blur(2.5px) is shallow but should be monitored in performance audits.

The existing .deck-gate input[aria-invalid] ring (line 770-772 in deck.css) uses --destructive, which may not be the same hue as --red-text; if inputs receive red-tinted borders, ensure the invalid state doesn't clash (test with a mistyped key).

deferredItems.item: Lock icon SVG asset (concentric circles, 'vault' metaphor)
deferredItems.why: Requires design asset work (SVG export, stroke/fill tuning, responsive scaling). Defer until visual spec is finalized. Current LockKeyhole glyph is functional; concentric design is nice-to-have for narrative cohesion.

deferredItems.item: Tailwind @theme alias for lock surfaces (--color-lock-surface-*)
deferredItems.why: Optional refactoring for future token maintainability. Current color-mix() expressions in deck.css are explicit and work; aliasing via Tailwind bridges is idiomatic but not blocking. Fold into a future glass-ui tokens audit (NEW wave) if token stability becomes a concern.

deferredItems.item: Homepage gallery ?export mode handling
deferredItems.why: The homepage is not typically exported (it's app chrome, not slide content). DeckGate must hide in ?export (blocked by the non-dismissable gate). Defer until export-mode requirements are clarified by the team.

findings.area: Frontend-design audit of dock chrome visuals (DeckView.vue + DeckSettings.vue + DeckPager.vue + deck.css §8; glass-ui DockIconButton + DropdownMenu + DarkModeToggle)
findings.summary: The dock chrome (GlassDock-hosted pager, navigation, settings, progress) demonstrates solid structural foundation but exhibits three distinct gaps in visual cohesion: (1) the pptx download submenu lacks theme indicator icons and visual hierarchy to distinguish light/dark exports, (2) the DarkModeToggle glyph at size="sm" (28px) reads noticeably undersized relative to the Home icon (18px lucide), creating a size hierarchy mismatch within the collapsed summary, and (3) the gauge/receipt visuals and progress-bar de-dock visual consequence remain unrefined at their current scales. The audit proposes idiomatic lucide-icon treatment for the download submenu, upsizing the DarkModeToggle to a "control" or "dock"-aware size tier, and fine-tuning gauge/progress scale relationships through @theme tokens rather than ad-hoc px.

findings.title: Download PPTX submenu lacks theme visual indicators
findings.evidence: DeckSettings.vue:53-72 — the DropdownMenuSub for 'Download PowerPoint' renders Sun/Moon icons (15px) but they are muted (--muted-foreground) with no tinted color and no affordance differentiation. deck.css:728-732 assigns color-mix() on .lucide-sun/.lucide-moon, but Sun gets portal-dot-amber and Moon gets ai-blue, making them visible only in context; the labels alone ('Light theme' / 'Dark theme') carry hierarchy.
findings.rootCause: The submenu icons inherit generic icon sizing (15px, hardcoded in template) with deck-global color tinting applied globally rather than as a popover-scoped treatment. No glass-ui DropdownMenu icon affordance pattern exists; the component treats icons as generic glyphs, not tier indicators.
findings.proposal: Replace hardcoded :size="15" with a scoped icon class that reads as a popover affordance. Tint Sun/Moon via CSS @utility or scoped class that lifts the deck's Sun→amber and Moon→ai-blue assignments into a popover context, making theme choice readable at a glance. The icons already carry the right semantic colors per deck.css §8; only the popover composition needs refinement to make them readable at their 15px size.

findings.title: DarkModeToggle glyph undersized relative to dock summary peers
findings.evidence: DeckSettings.vue:48 renders <DarkModeToggle size="sm" /> in the dock summary (collapsed state). dock.css:857-860 sets size="sm" → --dark-mode-toggle-size: 1.75rem (28px). DeckView.vue:145 renders Home icon via <DockIconButton> hosting <Home :size="18" />, a 18px lucide glyph. The 28px button housing an 18px icon reads visually balanced; the 28px toggle with its proportional SVG glyph reads noticeably smaller relative to the Home button's visual footprint.
findings.rootCause: DarkModeToggle.vue renders its SVG at width/height: 100% (filling the button), so the glyph scales with --dark-mode-toggle-size. At size="sm" (28px), the toggle reads as a secondary or tertiary accent rather than a peer to Home/Next/Prev. The user expectation is '~Home-glyph sized', implying visual equivalence, not 28px vs 40px edge-arrow targets.
findings.proposal: Change DeckSettings.vue from size="sm" to either size="control" or size="dock" (which auto-inherit the dock's --dock-control-size, 2.25rem at comfortable density, 2.5rem on coarse-pointer). This makes the toggle visually paired with DockIconButton's inherent sizing (both now read dock-native). Alternatively, expose a size="compact" tier (1.9rem) that matches the dock-pill visual moment without overscaling to full dock-control-size.

findings.title: Gauge and receipt sizing lack cohesive scale relation to dock and progress bar
findings.evidence: Slide07.vue:77-100 defines a 270° arc gauge with r=110, center (140,140) hardcoded in SVG viewBox="0 0 280 290"; Slide05.vue:37-55 renders a receipt-wrap with inline SVG perf (perforation) graphics. deck.css:654-680 governs the root .deck-progress bar (3px height, ::after fill driven by --p percentage). These three visual elements (gauge, receipt, progress) have no shared measure relation or token derivation; they sit at ad-hoc px scales orphaned from the deck's cqi/φ ladder.
findings.rootCause: Slide components authored SVGs with bare viewBox and hardcoded dimensions (rect widths, arc radii, line positions), not referencing deck tokens. No @theme binding or CSS var() anchors them to the φ-scaled measure system or to each other. The progress bar lives in a separate CSS file (deck.css) with no shared scale token.
findings.proposal: Introduce a `--deck-chrome-scale` token in deck.css §1 (alongside --cqx, --constellation-alpha, etc.) that acts as a measure knob for gauge/receipt SVG intrinsic sizes. Slides reference this token via CSS var() or via a composable (e.g., `useDeckScale()` returning the token value). The progress bar's ::after height could reference a derived `--progress-height` token (e.g., 3px base, scaled by --deck-chrome-scale). This keeps gauge, receipt, and progress in harmonic relation without per-slide hand-tuning.

findings.title: Dock summary hierarchy reads flat—no visual distinction between navigation tier and settings tier
findings.evidence: DeckView.vue:141-152 (#collapsed template) stacks Home · count/N · Settings in a single .deck-dock-summary flex row. All three are DockIconButton instances (or DarkModeToggle, which mirrors DockIconButton's glass surface). deck.css:684-696 styles .deck-dock-summary with flex gap:0.4rem; each element reads as equally prominent. No visual brake between the navigation anchor (Home) and the count register and the settings trigger.
findings.rootCause: The collapsed summary treats Home/count/Settings as a sequence with no hierarchy—no separator, no color differentiation, no scale variation. In contrast, the expanded state naturally separates these via .dock-separator and layout breathing room. The collapsed state collapses both spatially and semantically.
findings.proposal: Insert a visual brake (a subtle hairline or color shift) between the count register and the Settings gear to signal 'navigation unit' vs. 'utility controls'. Consider either: (a) a .dock-separator between count and gear (already used between nav and settings in expanded state; re-use here), or (b) a scoped opacity reduction on the Settings gear (opacity: 0.75, inheriting from dock-icon-button--muted, so it reads subordinate until hover). The separator is the idiomatic choice, keeping the visual grammar consistent with the expanded state.

findings.title: Progress bar de-dock visual consequence (collapse/expand transition) not articulated
findings.evidence: deck.css:654-680 pins .deck-progress fixed to the viewport bottom, z-index:40, behind the dock (z-index:50). The progress bar is independent of dock state (collapse/expand); it does NOT fade or scale or yield visual precedence when the dock collapses and expands. Only the dock pill transforms; the progress bar sits static beneath it. DeckView.vue:105-106 animates the fill width but not the bar's visibility or relationship to dock.
findings.rootCause: The progress bar and dock are visually orthogonal—no shared motion or state binding. When the dock collapses to a tiny pill, the progress bar still occupies its full bottom-viewport width, reading as a persistent chrome element that never tucks or breathes with the dock. On mobile with a tall dock (comfortable/spacious density), the progress bar may sit visually trapped under the dock without clear depth order.
findings.proposal: On collapsed state, fade the progress bar opacity to 0.5–0.65 (or hide it entirely) to yield visual dominance to the dock pill. On expand, restore full opacity in lockstep with the dock's morph animation (use the same --dock-motion-resize spring). Alternatively, when the dock is held open (dockRef.keepOpen()), the progress bar could fade to 0.4 opacity to signal 'the dock is the active surface now.' This is a gesture-UX refinement, not a breaking change—the progress bar remains functional, only its visual weight shifts.

risks: Changing DarkModeToggle size from 'sm' to 'control'/'dock' will widen the collapsed summary by ~4–6px, potentially pushing the summary off-screen on very narrow (<300px) viewports; verify --deck-pager-fit/@media ladder (deck.css:620-624) still fits 3-dot window. Mobile touch-target floors (dock.css:1180+) already account for 44px control-size; the change aligns with WCAG 2.5.8 and should NOT create overflow—the dock's own max-inline-size cap (deck.css:586) will clip gracefully.

Introducing --deck-chrome-scale token requires careful initialization: it must be set BEFORE slides render their SVG viewBox values (no runtime remeasure). Consider a composable or a slide-load hook if token is dynamic. If static, mint in deck.css §1 at 1.0, document the scale relationship for future slide authors.

The .deck-separator insertion between count and gear in collapsed state creates a visual axis shift vs. expanded state (separator sits between prev/next and pager in expanded, but between count and gear in collapsed). Verify the separator's line-height + color read consistently at both densities and both light/dark modes.
